Country of publication: India. *Āśaucyadīpikā*:
A lamp for impurity, possessing wicks made of the oil of agreeable Smṛti texts and the words of authoritative sages, to be accepted by the community of Śaivas.
I shall compose the *Āśaucadīpikā*.
For those whose bodies have been purified by initiation into the Śaiva Tantra— the source of the multitude of great scriptures that transcend all other systems—

and who constantly perform the worship of Śiva while bearing the burden of removing the world's suffering, there is no need to avoid the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*) when engaged in the supreme nectar-like practice of worshipping Śiva. In this specific case, the prohibitions regarding ritual impurity are set aside.

A certain lamp is being set forth, which illuminates the impurity that has become the object of thorough knowledge; its wick is the most stainless series of words from the excellent utterances of the authoritative ones, and it is held with affection by the mass of concordant Smṛtis. Herein—
The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that which speaks for the sake of establishing a single object beyond perception; therefore, Śiva is the supreme authoritative person (āptavara).
In the Pauṣkara:

"If this scripture (āgama), which is the word of a reliable authority (āpta), is now investigated, [it is found to be such] because of Ayurveda, because of the well-calculated nature of mantra-lore, and because of the efficacy taught by Rasasiddhas; thus it is authoritative."
It is thus accepted.
This authoritative word (*āptokti*) is also fourfold, according to the divisions of Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula. Among these as well—
The Śaiva Tantra is the most excellent; and its practice must not be performed with a confusion of Tantras. As it is said in the Makuta:
The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula systems constitute the fourfold [tradition]. Among these, the Śaiva is the most excellent, having originated from the Ūrdhvasrotas.

This tantra is the essence of the Vedas; therefore, one who follows the Vedic path should practice it. It consists of the meaning of the Vedānta, a knowledge that is the supreme and auspicious final doctrine.

The twenty-eighth [chapter] is the most excellent because it arises from the *ūrdhvasrotas* (the upward-flowing lineage). By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) as that "by which something is known," the *Jñānapāda* means a specific *tantra* that is a means for attaining knowledge. It should be understood as bestowing the essential meaning of the Vedas; other [parts], however, have different purposes.
The *Kāmika* states that what is effective is the Siddhānta, because it is the essence of the Vedas; anything else is excluded from the Vedas.
Conduct prescribed by the Siddhānta is called Vedic conduct.
Therefore, because the Śaiva Tantra originates from the *ūrdhvasrotas* (the upward stream),

because it is the cause of knowledge regarding the established tenets of Vedānta, and because other tantras convey different meanings, the practitioner of this [Śaiva Tantra] possesses precisely the status of a Vedic follower (*vaidika*).
Therefore, the practice of this tantra should be performed without confusion with other tantras.
For it is heard in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures that a fault arises if its practice is performed with confusion from other tantras.
This should be known as a division of Śaivism; one must not practice a mixture [of traditions].
Through the fault of mixing Tantras, the king and the kingdom perish.
There is no fault in the mutual intermingling of these twenty-eight tantras, beginning with the *Kāmika*; as it is said in the *Vīratantra*:
Thus, the Śaiva system is established with twenty-eight divisions; furthermore, one should consider the intermingling of these [divisions] not as a fault.

If it is argued that, in that case, since that Siddhānta is authoritative, it is logical that the Purāṇic statements composed by the divine people of Śiva should be included therein— no, because [it would also include] Smṛti statements, Purāṇas, and so forth that contradict it.

For even when something is to be abandoned, it is agreed that those statements which do not contradict it are to be accepted. As it is said in the Kāmika: "If it is to be performed, then that Śaiva action which is non-contradictory [to the higher teaching] should be practiced."
If something is contradictory, it should be abandoned; however, one must not abandon that which pertains to Śiva.
All that is Vedic which is not in contradiction with the Śaiva statements should be accepted;
it is said to be either Śaiva-Vedic or simply Vedic, or simply Śaiva.

The Śaiva [tradition] is both internal to and external to the Vedic; and that [Vedic tradition] is likewise [both internal to and external to] the Śaiva. Nevertheless, the Śaiva is superior to the Vedic, and there is nothing higher than it.

And for this *Dīpikā*, by means of illuminating the meaning of the words within the *Āśaucapada*, liberation (*mokṣa*)— which has as its goal the knowledge of what is to be avoided and what is prescribed by the feet of the Teacher— is the fruit; and those Śaivas who desire that [fruit] are the qualified candidates (*adhikārin*).
The Śaivas are of seven types.
As it is said in the Vīratantra (p. 329):
The Śaivas are to be known as being of seven kinds; hear now their distinctions:
the first is the Anādi-Śaiva, and the second is the Ādi-Śaiva.
The third is Mahāśaiva, the fourth is Anuśaivaka; the fifth is Vāntaraśaiva, and the sixth is called Pravara.
The seventh and the final one are said to be the divisions of the Śaivas:
the Anādi-Śaiva, the Saśiva, the Ādi-Śaiva, and the Śivadvija.
The Brāhmaṇa is indeed a Mahāśaiva, as are the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya;
the Śūdra is declared to be an Anuśaiva, and is considered to be of an intermediate status.
Those with six golden marks in the middle are known as Kulālas and Pāśvas; they are declared to be Pravara-Śaivas, and all of this has been told by me.
For other castes, the Antya-Śaiva is spoken of here.

Thus, these are the Anādi-Śaiva, Paraśiva, Ādi-Śaiva, Śiva-dvija, and Mahā-Śaiva Brahmins. Among them, the Śiva-dvija is born from the mouth of Brahmā through the very act of Śiva’s creation. The Mahā-Śaiva Brahmin, however, is born solely from the mouth of Brahmā without Śiva’s creative intervention. As it is stated in the Suprabheda:
Those Brāhmaṇas who were born on earth from the four faces of Brahmā, having arisen through the creation of Śiva,
are remembered as Śiva-Brāhmaṇas.

Since they are born solely from [his] mouth without the creative emission (*sṛṣṭi*) of Śiva, they are called ordinary Brāhmaṇas; one should lead them to Śiva through initiation. Thus [he is called] the *Ācārya*.
The remainder [is as follows]. Also in the *Kāmika*:
"But those who arise from the mouth of Brahmā without the creative emission (*sṛṣṭi*) of Śiva are common;
they do not possess the authority for the sake of the Supreme."
If, out of delusion, they should bring about the destruction of the king and the kingdom— thus [it is said regarding] the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are Śaivas; the intermediate Śaivas are the Śūdras,
while the Svarṇas, Ambaṣṭhas, Antaralikas, Kulālas, and Pāraśavas are the preeminent Śaivas.
"Beyond that are the *anyājātayaḥ* and the *antyaja-śaivas*"; here, the qualification belongs to those Śaivas who are distinct from the *anādi-śaivas*. Now, impurity (*āśauca*) is defined:
impurity is characterized by the unfitness for performing ritual action, and it resides in the person.

There is a certain lack of effort [regarding impurity], which is threefold due to its division into: that removable by time (*kālāpanodya*), that removable by bathing (*snānāpanodya*), and that removable by both time and bathing (*kālasnānāpanodya*). Among these, that removable by time refers to internal corpse-impurity (*antaraśava*) and village-impurity (*grāmāśauca*); in that case, it lasts until the corpse has departed from the village.

The impurity of the village lasts only for that duration; there is no requirement for bathing there, nor is the impurity caused by the death of a mere relative to be removed by bathing. There is no dependence on time for that [impurity], whereas the full period of impurity and the like are to be removed by bathing at the appropriate time—at the end of the period of affliction (*aghānte*).

Since bathing is impossible, this [impurity] is deficient; its causes are tenfold: birth, death, cremation, following the corpse, carrying it out, weeping, eating during the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), contact, not shaving, and not performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. In this regard:

A summary verse (saṃgrahaśloka): [He is characterized] by birth, death, cremation, following [the funeral procession], weeping, the removal of the corpse, the state of being a corpse, and liberation— [these occurring] nine, seven, and nine times respectively.
Is it not through the consumption of food that begins with the impure state of the womb and ends with death that one undergoes the activity of grasping an impure body day after day?

In this context, the sequence is not intended to be significant. Furthermore, birth is fourfold, distinguished as miscarriage (*garbhasrāva*), abortion (*pāta*), difficult delivery (*āpatprasava*), and easy delivery (*sukhaprasava*). Among these, miscarriage is the emergence of the fetus up until the end of the fourth month.

There is a miscarriage in the fifth and sixth months; beyond that, it is a birth of a corpse. From the tenth month onwards, there is an easy delivery. In those cases, as well as when there is a miscarriage from the mother's womb, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for as many days as the number of months [of pregnancy]. Thus, it is stated in the *Kāmika*:

Regarding the number of days corresponding to the month for the destruction of the fetus by a mother, whether female or male, a specific rule is stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*: "In the case of destroying the mother's fetus, three days are prescribed for up to three months; beyond that, until six months, four [days]."

Regarding the phrase "five or six days": according to this view, for up to three months, it is three days; for up to six months, it is a number of days equal to the number of months. Beyond that, the prescribed impurity for a woman who has given birth (*sūtikā*) occurs. In that context, this refers to the impurity of the *sūtikā* beyond [the first six months]. In that regard:
Regarding birth from a woman:

for the mother who has given birth to a female child, there shall be forty days; in the case of giving birth to a male, it should be known as thirty days; however, in the case of the birth of twins, it is said to be [forty-five].
In the case of a twin birth, when the semen is divided by the wind at the time of entering the womb, two forms arise.
As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"When, at the time [of conception], the semen within the womb is divided by the wind, it becomes two forms."
"Having gone, may he increase," thus says Śani.
And in the *Śaivapurāṇa*:
"When [the fetus] is repeatedly pierced by the wind, it becomes many according to its own nature. This refers to miscarriage (*srāva*) and falling out (*pāta*).
The bath for the father occurs at the very moment of death; the bath for the relatives occurs [at the end of the period of impurity].
As stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:

"In all cases, bathing is prescribed for the father starting from the fifth month, while for the relatives, bathing is required [at birth]. Here, birth is of three kinds: born dead (*mṛtajāta*), dead at birth (*jātamṛta*), and [the third type].
This is due to the distinction between those born [in a state of grace] and others. Among these, for the first two cases, purification for kinsmen occurs after ten days.
As it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*: "For one who has fallen [from grace], purification lasts until the fetus is full; for one who possesses knowledge, it is instantaneous."
In the *Kāmika*: "If the full embryo is destroyed, purification consists of knowledge that is instantaneous. Also in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Purification from the miscarriage of a full-term fetus occurs through knowledge in an instant; however, for the father, the period of impurity lasts ten days. As stated in the Kāmika:
"For the parents, there shall always be a ten-day period of impurity, as it is for all elder brothers. But in the Sujāta [Tantra]:
For paternal relatives and others, the period of impurity is full.

Easy delivery (*sukhaprasava*) is also of three kinds as previously described. Among these, in the first two cases, no ritual purification (*śauca*) regarding the branches [of the lineage] need be performed; rather, only the impurity due to birth (*jananāśauca*) must be observed. Consequently, the purification for the kinsmen (*jñātis*) following the birth is the same as in the case of a miscarriage (*avaprasava*). As stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"If one born alive dies, or if one dead is born,
one should not perform the impurity for the deceased, nor should one observe the impurity for birth."

For this very reason, even in the case of death from snakebite (*ādandaśāha*), the learned ones maintain that there is impurity for the relatives (*jñāti*) lasting until the day of the *sūti* (the birth-impurity period).
As stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"If the death of a newborn occurs within ten days, the impurity for the father is prescribed for the remaining days;
however, if the infant dies on the final day of those ten days or at dawn, the impurity lasts for two days."

Impurity occurs for three days in sequence; however, for the father, it lasts for two days, and on the final day, at dawn, there shall be three days. Now, regarding the case where a child dies at birth—there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śuddhi*).
But in the case of a stillbirth, the full impurity of childbirth (*sūtyā-śauca*) applies. This is the point here.

If it is argued that "kiliyāmakam" (the restrictive rule) is the [decisive factor], it should not be said that the statement "born alive" (*jīvan-jāta*) alone is the restrictor, for there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence (*prasakti*) [of impurity] even in the case of miscarriage. This is because it does not contradict statements from the *Kāmika* and other scriptures which prescribe immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) upon the loss of a full-term fetus. Nor, in that case, [is there any contradiction].

It should not be argued that even in the case of a miscarriage, the rule for the remaining days of impurity would not apply during the first ten days; for it is impossible to terminate the impurity that has already set in due to the powerful cause of death and birth, which pertains specifically to the destruction of a full-term fetus.

Furthermore, it is impossible to claim that the statements in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures refer to the state of miscarriage or half-death; therefore, enough of this digression. Even "well-born" [offspring] is of two kinds: the birth of a female and the birth of a male. Regarding the first, as for the girl who has been born...
The ten-day period of impurity (*daśāha-aśauca*) applies to the mother, father, their brothers, their sons, and paternal grandfathers.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*:
"Brothers, fathers, paternal uncles, and others are known as *bāndhavas*; those who are *jñātis* [are as follows]... [Regarding] *jñātis*...
When females are born, no period of impurity is prescribed.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti as well: "Upon the birth of a daughter, [the impurity falls upon] the brother, the father, the paternal uncle, and his sons.
And his paternal grandfather and brother are purified after ten nights.
Regarding the birth of a male child, however, there are three types of those subject to impurity:
those subject to full impurity, those subject to three-day impurity, and those subject to pakṣiṇī (two-day) impurity, [extending] through seven generations.

Up to the limit of the *sapiṇḍas*, they are subject to full impurity (*pūrṇāśauca*). Beyond that, up to the limit of five generations, the *samānodakas* are subject to three-day impurity (*tryahāśauca*). Further beyond, as far as the recognition of kinship (*bāndhava-parijñāna*), they are subject to impurity lasting for two days and a night (*pakṣiṇī*). As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
Impurity for those who have died or given birth is to be observed up to the seventh generation; beyond that, the impurity lasts for three days for all relatives within five generations.

Beyond that, a *pakṣiṇī* period is to be observed if it is known that the relative is still alive; furthermore, regarding the full duration of impurity: for Brāhmaṇas it is ten days, for Kṣatriyas twelve days, for Vaiśyas fifteen days, and for Śūdras one month.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"For a Brahmin, purification shall last ten days; for a Kṣatriya, twelve days;
for a Vaiśya, fifteen days; and for a Śūdra, one month."
And in the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa]:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, it shall be ten days; for a Kṣatriya, it shall be twelve days; for a Vaiśya, fifteen days; and for Śūdras, thirty days are prescribed."
And in the *Suprabheda*:
"Purification for a Brāhmaṇa occurs after ten days, for a Kṣatriya after twelve days; purification for a Vaiśya is said to be after a fortnight, and for a Śūdra after a month."
In the *Ṣaṭsahasrikālottara*:
"A twice-born man who remains for ten days [without initiation] has no authority here in the performance [of rites]; [if he remains] for twelve days..."
And a Vaiśya who kills a king shall be purified by fifteen days [of penance].

Regarding the statement, "The Śūdra is purified by the cessation of recitation and meditation," there is a contraction of this impurity based on caste according to the stage of life (*āśrama*). For example, for the student (*brahmacārī*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), purification is immediate (*sadyaśśauca*), but not so for the householder (*gṛhastha*).
There is no restriction whatsoever; for there being a lack of evidence to restrict it,

once all four castes (*varṇa*) have taken up the *śivāśrama* by resorting to Śaivism, [they are entitled] to each caste's fourfold [initiation], namely the *samaya*, *viśeṣa*, *nirvāṇa*, and *abhiṣeka*.
There are people known as *samādhiputra*, *sādhaka*, and *ācārya* who arise in succession.

The *samayin*, the initiated (*dīkṣita*), the *sādhaka*, and the final *guru*—these four castes (*varṇas*) are established in their respective positions according to their specific application. Among those four castes:

For the *sādhaka* and the *ācārya*, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*). For the *samadhī* and the *putraka*, however, among the Ādiśaivas, Mahāśaivas, and Anuśaivas, there is never any restriction regarding the period of impurity prescribed according to their caste. But for the Avāntaraśaivas, there is indeed a restriction on that [period] for the *samadhī* and the *putraka*.

For the spiritual son (*putraka*) as well, there is immediate purity (*sadyaśśauca*) at the time of worship among all castes. In that regard, there are two kinds of initiates (*samayin*): those devoted solely to the twilight prayers (*sandhyopāsanā*), and those who are also intent upon the rites of Śiva. Among them, for the first kind of initiates...

For the intermediate Śaivas— who possess only the practice of daily bathing, recitation, and meditation, who are devoted to the performance of ritual bathing and recitation, and who are devoid of temple duties—
the period of impurity lasts twenty-five nights.
336) The intermediate [attainment] for those who perform the conduct consisting of service to Śiva— such as sweeping and plastering in the temple according to the rules—
is like the practice of the path of servitude (dāsamārga) taught by the Lord’s feet.
For the second class of Śaivas, the *samayins*, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts twenty nights; likewise, in the *Kāmika*:
"But for those devoted to the rites of Śiva who are associated with ashes and so forth, [the status of] Śūdras..."
"Pure in twenty days, the supreme [form] in twenty-five"—
thus it is said here:
"The thorough cleansing of Maheśvara, who is the embodiment of action, should be performed gradually by those well-composed in their devotion."
While sweeping with a soft, fine broom.
One should take pure cow dung and smear it upon the abode of Śaṅkara; then, having taken up white flowers born from oneself, one should worship him.
He who, having taken up a garland, should offer it endowed with auspiciousness;
he who should perform everything such as hymns and songs—all this is the path of service (*dāsamārga*).
In the *Śivajñānabodhasaṃgraha*, the path of service is expressed by the term "Śiva-activity" (*śivakarma*). [The rest of the text follows.]

By this, others who are devoid of the path of the servant (dāsa-mārga) have been described. For the "spiritual sons" (putrakas)— who possess the purificatory rites of special initiation, wear sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, and perform the worship of Maheśvara— there is no impurity during birth or death among these intermediate Śaivas.
The period of impurity is fifteen days. As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"And those Śūdras who are devotees of Maheśvara and wear the sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads—for them, purification from birth or death [impurity] shall occur after fifteen days."
"Māheśvaras" means those who perform the worship of Maheśvara. And in the *Svāyambhuva*:
"For those devoted to Śiva who worship the Liṅga, one should observe impurity for a fortnight.

Thus it is said. And in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "A Śūdra who does not drink liquor, is of noble birth, and is constantly devoted to dharma, may become initiated; otherwise, [this occurs] after one fortnight or one month."
However, the two types of *pravara-śaiva* and *antyaja-śaiva* are to be considered:

even though the specific *samayas* (observances) of those two [lower classes] are not possible, there is no restriction on their respective intermediate Śaiva-nature as members of their own castes who have been initiated (*samayin*). This is because there is no authoritative evidence for such a restriction.

Now, one might object: "Since Smṛti texts such as 'In the Kali age, impurity due to sequence and impurity due to qualities are cast far away,' etc., even for an intermediate Śaiva, the impurity based on being a *samayin* or a *putraka* must likewise be cast away as an impurity of quality; and the Kāmika and other scriptures are the authority for this, as follows:"
Likewise, for those who know the Śiva Āgamas and those who dwell in the Śiva-āśrama; as it is stated in the Śivadharma:
"For all castes indeed, those who dwell in the Śiva-āśrama..."
The Śivadharma, spoken by Śiva, [leads] to dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, woman, or Śūdra, one who has entered the Śiva-āśrama—
be he a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—
for such as these consecrated by the initiation of Nirvāṇa, no impurity (sūtaka) exists at all.
For this observer of the Śiva-vow, there is neither death nor ritual impurity.

"For one who abides by the *samaya*, there is never impurity regarding the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*); however, regarding optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), there is impurity, which ceases upon bathing. (p.

In the *Kālottara* and other such texts, it is understood that for those initiated into *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*, there is an absence of *sūtaka* (impurity); yet in those very same texts, through passages such as "therefore, even by worldly initiates," the existence of *sūtaka* for those very individuals is also understood. And so:

If it is argued that the description of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for both the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*) applies even across all castes (*sarvavarṇa*), we reply: this is because the authority of both types of statements is established by their being proclaimed by Śiva.

The mutual contradiction arising from the conceptualization of differences within the initiation for Nirvāṇa must be resolved. On this very point, the teacher Jñānaśaṅkarācārya, the author of the *Bālaratnāvalī*, having raised an objection, [states] the teachers’...
Furthermore, even in the case of a second cremation, the period of impurity lasts ten nights for all castes alike,
whether it be due to birth or death.
"Śātātapa declared that purification occurs in ten days;
however, for Śūdras who are devoid of mantras, the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) takes place on the twelfth day."
The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) likewise ordained that this must always be performed by the giver.
The sage Aṅgiras stated:
"A disciple and a servant who have died [shall receive their portion] after the passing of their respective funeral cakes (piṇḍas), as well as the preceptor and the master."
"Equal impurity" refers to those residing in that same family.

Having conceptualized a distinction based on whether one follows the *lokadharmiṇī* initiation for Nirvāṇa through the practice of the Śiva- and Mala-related duties, or the *stanadharmiṇī* initiation for the world of Sadāśiva through the practice of the Stanaloka-related duties, or whether one maintains separate cooking during the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) or does not.
Thus, the mutual contradiction between the statements regarding the presence and absence of *sūtaka* (impurity) has been resolved.
Accordingly, for those initiated by the *Śivadharmiṇī* [initiation], there is the world of Sadāśiva and the other [higher realms];
and for those initiated by the *Lokadharmiṇī*, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) for those who maintain their own separate cooking fires.
p.
339) For those who have been initiated into Nirvāṇa and are thus free from the [distinction between] separate [castes], the rule regarding birth-impurity (sūtaka) no longer applies;
this is solely by virtue of their reliance on initiation into the Śiva-dharma.
Thus, it is not unreasonable to say that immediate purification (*sadyaśśauca*) is prescribed for those who have taken the *samaya* [initiation]. Now, if it is asked:
"In that case, how many days of impurity (*āśauca*) apply to those who have been initiated into *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā* and yet still possess *sūtaka*?"—the answer is as follows:
among the Ādi-Śaivas, Mahā-Śaivas, Anu-Śaivas, and Avāntara-Śaivas...
For all of them, the period of impurity lasts for only three days. As stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:
"There is no loss [of status], nor separate cooking; his impurity is removed, O Śivātmikā.
Also in the *Kālottara*:
Every day, one should perform the three oblations of the Antaryāga; on the fourth day, however, it must be performed as a daily rite (nitya) in the same manner as before.

Nor should it be said that the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) is not being taught here, and therefore the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) is being prescribed; for the prescription of the internal sacrifice—which is inherently inseparable from it—serves as the indicator (*gamaka*) of that impurity.
Furthermore, since for those who observe the commitments (*samayin*) during a period of impurity only the external sacrifice is prescribed, there is no [need for] the internal sacrifice.

It must be said that the injunction is logical. However, the injunction for internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) is inappropriate there, because it is impossible to perform it due to the frequent perception [of obstacles].

If it is argued that, therefore, both types of statements lack authority due to their mutual contradiction, we say no; for [the means are] devotion, knowledge, and dispassion (*bhakti-jñāna-vairāgya*).
For the establishment [of the rules] is justified by both firmness and wealth. And it is said in the *Kāmika*:
"Whether devotion, knowledge, or detachment—whichever of these one may possess perfectly—it is with that that the worship of the *samayin* should be performed."
p.

340) "Even for one for whom these three [faculties] are dull or even very dull, the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) must still be performed"— therefore, this applies to all four Śaiva systems from the beginning.
For those who have been initiated into Nirvāṇa and are devoid of separate ritual cooking, the period of impurity is three nights.

For those among the intermediate Śaivas who are merely *samayins* (bound by the rules) through the performance of the twilight devotions (*sandhyopāsti*) alone, it is twenty-five days. For a *samayin* devoted to the rites of Śiva, the period of impurity is twenty days.
It is faultless that for the *putraka* it lasts fifteen days;
likewise for the Rudra-kanyās, the five beginning with Nakra, and the five Ācāryas, it is fifteen days.
This is stated in the Kāmika:
Likewise, it is agreed that there is a five-day observance for the daughters of Rudra;
however, in the *Candrajñāna*,
a fourteen-day period for the daughters of Rudra is stated, as follows:
Impurity due to birth and impurity due to death are purified after fourteen days.
Regarding the five types of teachers, they are those mentioned in such passages as: "The dancer, the bard, the singer, and likewise the flute-player," and so forth.
In the *Kāmika*, it is stated that for those who perform Drāviḍa singing as prescribed by the Āgamas, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is waived for fifteen days;
likewise for those who possess knowledge of Śiva and those who dwell in the Śiva-āśrama.

The purification for temple-maidens (*devadāsī*), however, occurs after twenty days. Likewise, in the *Kāmika*, it is proclaimed: "The purification of a temple-maiden is declared to take place in twenty days.
But in the *Candrajñāna*, it is stated that the period of impurity for a temple-maiden lasts until the end of a fortnight (*pakṣānta*).
Impurity due to birth and impurity due to death are purified in ten days;
this is also stated in the *Svāyambhuva*:

The specific impurity for the daughters of Rudra and others has been particularly shown: for the courtesans of Rudra and those two [other classes], the impurity lasts thirteen days; for ascetics and temple-prostitutes, the impurity lasts one fortnight.
And there are exactly fifteen Viṣṇudāsīs and Kadāsīs.
Herein, the nature, duties, and impurity of the Rudrakanyās and Devadāsīs have been explained in detail in the *Kāraṇa*.
Dattā, Kṛtābhibhūtā, Bhaktā, Amṛtā, Alaṃkāradāsikā, and Rudrakanyā—
these seven have been appointed to my service.
She who is given by her own kinsmen in a matter such as plowing and so forth to one who possesses devotion is known as "given" (dattā);
now hear the characteristics of the "bought" (krītā).
She who is given away for the purpose of servitude by her devotee— whether out of greed for wealth or having received money—
is declared to be "sold."
She who sings at my palace for the sake of the death of a family member shall become a slave for her livelihood;
she is called a *cihnitābhibhūtaka*.
She who, being a devotee of Śambhu, thinks "I myself am His servant," and bears the marks [of devotion] upon her body— she indeed is called a *bhakta*.
The girl who was previously established here as a maidservant in my house has died somewhere due to agitation; another image of Kālārcā has been installed here by the preceptors.
Now it is said that a female servant, having been offered by those who were attached, died;
she was made to perform singing and dancing by the actors, being highly trained therein.
Another woman was teaching in a royal drama school;
adorned with ornaments, she was a most beautiful young girl.
Furthermore, for the sake of pleasing me, the Lord of the Mountain, she shall have the marks of service performed upon her in the temple;
she shall be a female servant who assists in all tasks.
The beautiful wives of the sages, having been abandoned by them due to contact with me, were remembered as the daughters of Rudra when they came to dwell in my house.
Thus described, these various kinds of maidservants are seen in my abode; in this world of abundant merit, they are devoted to my service.
As for those [women] who have been handed down through lineage, how could there be a limit to their merit? But those women of mixed birth who are pure are indeed excellent wives.
Those who are marked [with the appropriate signs] should perform the works of my temple;
furthermore, according to the rules for initiation (dīkṣā), there is a distinction of characteristics among these [women].
Likewise, there is a division among them according to their respective functions;
for those who are the attendants of Rudra, there is no such thing as birth and so forth.
Singing and dancing at night are prescribed as their duties;
now hear of the respective duties of the other celestial courtesans.
The preceptor performs the rites of sweeping, sprinkling, smearing, and applying powder; he also oversees the bringing of rice, the cleansing of vessels, and the singing and dancing.
The playing of flutes, lutes, and so forth, as well as [other musical activities], whether out of suspicion,
pride, lineage, or for any other reason;
One should have all rites performed, especially by the daughters of Rudra;
and those born of mixed castes who are known as "my female servants" (mama-dāsyaḥ).
Women wearing washed garments shall perform all rites;
among them, she who is renowned here as Sarvasumāmadasi shall [be employed].
Listen to the prescribed rites for his daughters, granddaughters, and others: the wearing of the auspicious thread must be performed in the presence of Śiva.
And for men who have come down through tradition without distinction, the status of being a Brāhmaṇa is considered equal in matters such as the wearing of garments and other such practices.
And the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) preceded by initiation into Śiva.

In the case of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka), there is mutual impurity for half a month; in that [period], the sequence is as follows: the Three-eyed One [Śiva] removes it in three days, and Hari [Viṣṇu] in one day.
In all cases, whether there is a death or a birth, the impurity lasts for ten days; there is no distinction between woman and man based on age, such as being old or young.

And there exists the knowledge of a single family; as long as that [knowledge] persists, it shall be half [of the full]. But in the absence of their daughters, having taken [the lineage] from a woman of the *lotabha* caste—
The instructor should have the ritual acts performed by that maiden according to the prescribed rite, as well as by female attendants such as Rudrakanyās,
and by male dancers.
For those women, there would be two families, one prior and one subsequent;
for those born of the same lineage and caste, the middle [family] would likewise exist.

344) Furthermore, according to the *Gotrasūtra*, for those of the highest birth who have been given [in adoption],
as well as for ancestors, full impurity is prescribed in the former case.
The lineage-sūtra (gotrasūtra) of Āsā is not accepted by the supreme teacher; therefore, that which is born from the lineages of the former and the latter is to be practiced as inferior.
Even for those given away through a subsequent marriage alliance, the period of impurity lasts fifteen days.
In the case of birth or death among maternal relatives and close kinsmen, the period of impurity for one another shall be fifteen days; this applies equally to those such as Pāraśavas and others.
Just as for ascetics, [impurity] lasts only as long as the connection with their seeds [of lineage], so for those related by birth or marriage,
it is ordained for half a month.
For Rudrakanyā and other female attendants, as well as for Pāraśava Śaiva ascetics, the period of impurity shall be half of fifteen days— that is, seven and a half days—
and ignorance [of the rules] shall apply in both cases.
For those who have been given away and have attained both [states], there exists the status of the supreme teacher; therefore, for the temple-maidens (devadāsīs), the impurity lasts for one month.

However, those who have been assigned to the various classes of female servants within the temple (karmandira) are not distinct from that [temple]; therefore, they are devoid of any connection with the lower [worlds].
Among those [women], such as appointed daughters (putrikā) and others, mutual marriage is desired; and there is no impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (bhūta) for them in either of the two lineages.
Due to their connection, there is proximity within a single location;
from that proximity, the inevitability of touch and so forth arises through fear.
p.
345) Therefore, in the absence of a [maternal] connection, a two-day period of impurity is prescribed;
however, that shall be full [ten days] as long as there is death in both lineages.
Therefore, apart from the nature of the gift, what other proof, experience, or basis for certainty is there? Without approval, one should perform actions together with the mother who accepts them.
When a Brāhmaṇa has performed the marriage rite with women of the four castes, then,
upon the death of a Brāhmaṇī wife or upon the birth of a son, the impurity for the husband lasts three days.
In the case of a Śūdra woman’s death, as well as upon the birth of her son, the husband has one day of impurity.

For sons of Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya women, in the event of the death of their respective mothers, or upon the birth or death of those respective sons, the period of impurity is that which is prescribed for the caste of each respective mother.
Having abandoned the purchased wife and the excellent wife, this tradition extends as far as two generations;
for those of lower status, it is thus remembered that the period is half a month.
Due to the contraction of their [status], the destruction of their position is certain.

Therefore, for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, one must act after careful examination; for he who, out of delusion or through hypocritical conduct, performs what is contrary to that which is prescribed for his own caste [is ruined].
Having performed [the rite], one should go home; otherwise, the destruction of the site will certainly occur.
To pacify that fault, one should perform expiatory rites (prāyaścitta).
Therefore, with every effort, one should properly observe the period of impurity (*āśauca*).
In the *Kāmika*:
"When four women have been married by a Brāhmaṇa, the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) [applies] in successive order..."
The period of impurity (*sūtaka*) for their sons and others is ten, six, three, or one day, according to the opinion regarding the mother’s side. (p. 345b)

In the *Kiraṇa* as well, there is a verse to this effect: "For Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have been raised according to the prescribed rule, purification occurs after eleven, twelve, thirteen, and [fourteen] days respectively upon the death of their husbands;
likewise, for a Kṣatriya [wife], it is fourteen days."

Purification occurs after fifteen days for a Śūdra woman married by a Vaiśya; purification occurs after eighteen days for a Śūdra woman married by a Vaiśya. Regarding the three women of the Kṣatriya and other castes who have been taken as wives by Brāhmaṇas and others without [following] the prescribed rites:

Upon the death of their husbands, women undergo a period of impurity for one, two, three, or four days beyond the number of days prescribed for the caste of their own husband. This is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"In the case of a Brahmin [husband], among the three wives wed according to the prescribed rites who are devoted [to him]..."
Through practice for one, two, or three days, [the powers of] the dull-witted and others [arise] starting from the Brāhmaṇa caste and so forth.
That which is born from an improper union is impure; it becomes fit [for ritual use] after two or three Vedic days have passed.
Here, the word "Veda" does not denote the number four as a count of elements.
Among those born in the direct order (anuloma), the son of a woman of the same caste is the *savarṇa*, while the son of a *pārāśava* woman is the sixth.
For one's maternal relatives who are *ugra*, *pūtīka*, and so forth—six in total—the impurity lasts for two or three fortnights.
This occurs by adding one, two, or three days beyond the number of days of impurity belonging to the paternal side.
As it is stated in the *Svāyaṃbhuvasmṛti*:
One born to a Brahmin from a king’s daughter is named Savarṇa;
his period of impurity lasts eleven days, and he should perform his duties like a twice-born.
One born from a Brahmin father and a Vaiśya maiden is called an Ambaṣṭha;
for him, the impurity due to birth and death lasts for ten days.
The same principle should be understood to apply to the respective mothers of the others as well.
The nature of the *anuloma* [deities], however, has been described in the *Suprabheda*.
One should know that the first is the Savarṇa, the second is the Ambaṣṭha, and the third is the Pāraśava; these are born from a Brāhmaṇa.
Maddhara and Ugrana are born as the two [sons] of the king; Cūcuka is to be known as the [son] of the Vaiśya, and there are six including Sasvalulomaṇ.
Thus, having obtained the princess according to the prescribed rite with the recitation of mantras, a son of equal caste was born there;
he is honored among those born of marriages in the direct order (anuloma).
From the union of a Brahmin with a Vaiśya woman, the sixth [caste], named the Ambaṣṭha, is born; from the union of a Brahmin with a Śūdra woman, one born is known as the Pāraśava.
One born from a red man and a yellow woman is known as Madgu; one born from a black woman through union with a red man is known as Ugra.
From the union of black and yellow, one born is indeed a *śūcuka*.
It is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) belongs to the male and female servants, while that which is appropriate for the lineage of the presiding deity [belongs to the master]. (Thirteen)
A deceased Brāhmaṇa is declared pure after ten days; a Karaka, a Kolaka, and a cowherd are considered pure after thirty days;
and both a Bhaṭṭa and an Ācārya become pure after thirty-four days.
If purification occurs after thirty-five days, one becomes pure by using betel, lotuses, and oil indicated by the speech of a potter; if after thirty-six days, one is purified by these means.
Regarding these [occupations], beginning with the sale of liquor and ending with the sale of oil, the period of impurity (āśauca) has been clearly stated in the *Candrajñāna* (p.
Now listen to the impurity regarding messengers: the birth-impurity lasts for thirty days;
the death-impurity is purified after thirteen days. For Karakola, the birth-impurity and the death-impurity are both purified after thirty days. For Gopāla, it is the mantra-impurity.
Impurity due to death is purified in thirty days; for Bhaṭṭārya, impurity due to birth or death lasts thirty days. For others, it is all types of impurity.
As stated in the Kāmika:

"There is no impurity regarding those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), because they are eternally pure. Thus, for birth, the period of birth-impurity has passed; there is no birth-impurity [for them]. For a father, it is thirty-six days.
For a washerman, it is thirty-six days. And for a seller of oil, it is also thirty-six days.

For others, there is full impurity; for a potter it is thirty-six days, for a mason thirty-five days; for a slanderer thirty-five days, for a backbiter thirty-six days, and for a betel-seller thirty-six days.
For a washerman, there is impurity for thirty-six days; for an oil-seller as well, thirty-six days.
Regarding others, all types of impurity have been stated in the *Kāmika*:
"In the case of those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), there is no impurity, because they are eternally pure."
When birth has passed, there is no impurity (āśauca) due to birth. Regarding the father’s bath, it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"The father’s bath [occurs] at that time, but for others it does not [occur] until the end of the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Death is of two kinds.
—Easy death and difficult death. The first is of two kinds: the death of a woman and the death of a man. "Death of a man" means [death] that occurs immediately.
For a Kṣatriya woman, there is one day of impurity prior to birth, and likewise for the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*).
Upon her death, it is ten days; upon the birth of her son, it is six days.
For a Vaiśya woman, upon her death, it is one day prior to the husband's performance of the marriage rites; upon the birth of her son, it is likewise.
Prior to the *upanayana*, it is even slightly more than that; after the *upanayana*, there is full impurity (*pūrṇāśauca*). Likewise, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Until the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), there is one day of impurity; until the eruption of teeth, one day; for the *cūḍā* ceremony, three days."
That vow has been declared to be exceedingly superior.
Beyond that, for all castes, this is the rule regarding prior purification:
according to the *Kāmika*,
from birth until the eruption of teeth, and thereafter until the time of initiation (*upanayana*), the bath is to be performed on a single day.
And it is declared that this should be done for three days in sequence.
"Beyond that, for the relatives, it shall be ten days. However, in the *Kāmika*, a specific rule is stated regarding Kṣatriyas and others whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has been completed:
"When a Kṣatriya's tonsure has been completed, he becomes pure in six days; but a Vaiśya..."
A Śūdra becomes pure after nine days, or after twelve days.

Since it is indicated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī* that it is even greater than that because of being "obscured" (*āvṛta*), therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa as well, there is impurity (*āśauca*) lasting four or five days after the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) and before the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). This applies to the Brāhmaṇa.

The tying of the muñja-grass girdle is the *upanayana* for a Kṣatriya, the taking up of the bow for a Vaiśya, and the undertaking of the vow (*vratodagrahaṇa*) for others; according to the duration of these respective ages, there is full impurity. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*:

For a Brahmin, [the impurity] lasts three days until the tying of the girdle (*mauñjī-bandhana*); for a Kṣatriya, until the taking up of the bow; for women, it is said to be from the time of shaving [the head]; and for those of the eighth caste (Śūdras), it is as before, starting from marriage respectively. In the case of the death of a maiden who has been betrothed but not yet married...

"Beyond three nights, for a female relative who has been given away but not yet married, the [period of impurity] is the same as for one who has died. Beyond that, however, there is no *sāpiṇḍya* at all for a maiden; everything must be performed within the husband's family alone. And so it is stated in the *Candrajñāna*:
For those who have entered another lineage, it is held that the inheritance and the period of impurity cease; it is said that all kinship in that family comes to an end.
And whatever impurity belongs to that woman's husband, that same impurity applies to her as well. Thus it is stated in the *Candrajñāna*:
"Whatever impurity belongs to the husband, there is no doubt that it is the same for the wife. In this regard:

In all cases of the death of a male prior to the *upanayana* ceremony, as well as in all cases of the death of a female prior to marriage, there is a ten-day period of impurity (*āśauca*) for both the mother and the father; furthermore, after the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) has been performed, brothers also observe a ten-day period. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
For brothers, the period of impurity shall last ten days, but only if the funeral rites have been performed, not at all times;
for parents, it shall likewise be ten days, but for elder brothers, the impurity lasts at all times.

In this regard, concerning the three-day impurity of the *sapiṇḍas*, there is one day of impurity for those belonging to the *samānodaka* group; and in the case of that one-day impurity, there is merely bathing. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*:

(350) According to the sacred law, the period of impurity prescribed for sapinda relatives is three days, while for those belonging to the group of samānodaka relatives, it is one day wherever they may reside.

It is proclaimed that for them, bathing is prescribed prior to the eruption of the upper teeth; "from the eruption of the teeth" refers to the period of one day (*ekāha*). This impurity (*āśauca*) regarding the death of a maiden or a child is common to all castes (*varṇa*). Thus it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
And in the Smṛti it is stated: "This rule applies to all castes," and "The period of impurity based on age is declared to be equal for all castes.
Therefore, in the event of deaths occurring prior to the initiation ceremony (upanayana), there is no period of impurity for those who share the funeral rice-ball (sapinda).
For the mother, the father, and siblings, it is stated that the period of impurity (āśauca) lasts for three nights or three months. And thus says the author of the Saṃgraha:
"In the Smṛti, [impurity] occurs for the parents and brothers, but for others it is lower, provided they have not been initiated."
Impurity (*aśauca*) has been declared to be based on the impurities of childhood (*bālāsaṃskāra*). As the author of the *Saṃgraha* states:
"In the case of cremation, [impurity lasts for] one day; in the case of burial, immediately; after the eruption of teeth, [it lasts for] three days; in the case of burial, [it lasts for] three days;
and in the case of cremation and abandonment [of the body], three days are prescribed."
The specific time for the *saṃskāra* (funerary rite) is stated in that very same [text]:
"After the *caula* and before the naming ceremony (*nāma*), burial is prescribed;
or else, after the eruption of teeth, either cremation or burial may take place."
The entire nature of the procedures for cremation and excavation is to be found in the Caryāpāda section of the *Suprabheda*.
Following the initiation (*upanaya*), there are five types of those subject to ritual impurity (*āśauca*):
those with full impurity, those with three-day impurity, and those with impurity lasting for two nights (*pakṣiṇī*).
There are those who observe impurity for a day and those who observe immediate purification.
Regarding birth, the *sapinda* relatives of the father and others observe full impurity.
Furthermore, the full period of impurity for a Brāhmaṇa by means of ten days and so forth has already been stated previously in the *Kāmika*:
"In the case of death or birth, [the impurity] is to be observed up to the seventh generation of those men. From that, five...
Those who share the same water-libation (samānodaka) until the seventh generation (puruṣaparyanta) are subject to impurity for three days;
likewise, students and relatives are subject to impurity for three days. Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
"Beyond that [seventh generation], there is impurity for three days up to the fifth person; [then] for the student alone..."
Those who are related to the guru, as well as those who are related to the guru's relatives.
They should abandon for three days all ritual acts other than the obligatory ones, such as *japa* and so forth.
The eight persons who must be present nearby are: the maternal grandmother, the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the mother’s sister’s son, and the daughters of one’s mother’s sisters.

Those subject to three-day impurity (*tryahāśaucin*): upon the death of a woman, the mother, father, one’s own daughter, daughter’s son, sister’s son, husband’s sister’s son, and the wife of a grandson are subject to three days of impurity when in the presence of six persons. This is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:

"And for a sister's son and a daughter's son, it is prescribed for three days when they have died"—this meaning, which was explained from the beginning, is stated here in a summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*) for the sake of easy understanding:
"Upon the death of a male [relative], the mother and father [are impure]; the daughter and the daughter's son [are impure] for three days."

"Your [impurity] lasts for three days regarding those who are present, with the husband's sister's son as the sixth"—the meaning of "regarding those who are present" (*pratyakṣe*) is "when they are visibly present. Those whose kinship is known are subject to impurity for the duration of a *pakṣinī* (fortnight). As it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "As long as they are known [to be related]."

Upon the death of a woman, thirty-eight people; upon the death of a man, twenty-six people who are related by birth (yonisaṃbandha) are subject to impurity for a period of one fortnight. For instance, in the case of a woman's death, there are four in the lineage of the father’s father.

352) In the case of Janaka, there are eight [factors] in its own category (*svakoṭi*), fifteen in its own-produced category (*svajanyakoti*), six in its own-and-its-produced category (*svasvajanyakoti*), and four in its seven-fold own-produced category (*saptasvajanyakoti*). [This applies to] the male at the time of death.
Two in the category of the father’s father, four in the category of the father’s father’s father; four in the category of oneself;

and two in the category of one’s own offspring—adding these twelve sapindas to the twenty-six previously mentioned persons, there are thirty-eight who are subject to impurity for three days (*pakṣiṇī*). This is stated in the *Saṃgraha*: [text follows].
The summary verse explaining the meaning of [the list beginning with] "mother's sister, daughter, son," and so forth,
is stated for the sake of easy understanding:
"Mother, father, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, likewise mother's sister, maternal uncle's wife."
The wife of one's father’s brother, the father’s sister;

the wife of one’s mother’s sister, of one’s maternal uncle, of one’s father’s brother, and of one’s father’s sister; the wife of one’s son, a daughter-in-law, a paternal aunt, a sister, and her husband.
One's own sister’s daughter-in-law, one's own daughter, and also one's son's daughter; one's own granddaughter, one's own daughter's daughter, and that daughter's husband's wife.

"In these cases, for thirty-eight persons, there is a *pakṣiṇī* [period of impurity] upon the death of a woman; among these, for twelve who are *sapiṇḍas*, it is as stated, and for others, it is likewise upon the death of a man. And in the *Kāmika*:
"Upon the death of a married woman, of one's mother or father, upon the death of a uterine sister, or upon the death of a brother or a sister's son..."
She was bestowed upon her maternal uncle as his wife.
For example,
O best of the twice-born, when a woman who has given birth dies, there is a period of impurity lasting for one night (pakṣiṇī) for her parents and siblings, and generally for her sons as well.
Thus, "given" means "married. For two *pakṣiṇī* days, there is either two nights or two days;
that is, one night and one day, or two nights and two days.
As it is said in the Kāmika:
"The night situated between two days, or the day situated within the night, is called 'pakṣiṇī' (the bird-day); having understood this, one should perform the ritual."

However, for those who are pure after one day (*aharāśocin*), the previously mentioned [periods] are indeed those of impurity for a female relative (*pakṣiṇī*). Those who are pure after one day [apply] when [the death] is out of sight (*parokṣe*). As it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"In the case of blood relations (*yonisambandha*), the rule of one day applies when [the death] is not present."

Those who stand on the Śaiva path but are distinct from the relationship of disciple and teacher, even if they have received initiation (*dīkṣita*), are subject to impurity for one day. As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Others than those [the former], whether householders or even non-householders, who stand on the Śaiva path, [are purified after] one day."
Those associated with destruction and effort are intended for the sake of purification.

Thus, this rule regarding the three-day and one-and-a-half-day periods is common to all castes. It is stated in the *Saṃgraha*: "For those who are immediately purified (*sadyaśśaucin*), there is bathing for the mother, the father, the guru, and others who share the water [of the funeral rite]; however, in the case of the mother's siblings and peers, it is equal to that of a person of the same caste."

"Vijñāneśvara has declared [this] regarding kinsmen (bāndhava)," because it was established by the female bird for her own kinsmen; thus it is stated in the Saṃgraha that "the three types of kinsmen are the relatives.
The nature of these three kinds of kinsmen has been demonstrated by Vijñāneśvara.

One who has been initiated should not practice such things as these among the species of sacrificial animals. However, if his body is extremely afflicted or tormented by the exhaustion of his faults, he may then take the consent of virtuous teachers and Brahmins.
Having reflected upon the duty appropriate for that time, one should perform the rite preceded by expiation;

even then, there is no impurity (*sūtaka*), for one becomes purified simply by bathing. This applies to the student (*brahmacārī*), whether a *bhautika* or a *naiṣṭhika*, as well as to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and the ascetic (*yati*), in the event of the death of a sapinda relative.
Furthermore, there is no impurity (aśauca). As it is stated in the *Prodvīta*:

"A celibate student (*brahmacārī*), one who wears matted hair (*jaṭādhārī*), a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) free from impurity, as well as a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and an ascetic (*yati*), should always avoid impurity."
And in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Of those who are lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), forest-dwellers (vānaprastha), ascetics (yati), and students (brahmacārin)..."

Nor should one shed tears, offer funeral cakes, or perform the śrāddha and other such rites.
Even for one initiated into the Śivadharmiṇī [initiation], there is no impurity (āśauca). It is stated in the Kāmika:

"For this bearer of the Śiva-vow, there is neither death nor birth-impurity (sūtaka), because of his independence from prior [worldly] considerations and because he is the cause of the withdrawal of worldly existence."
And in the *Suprabheda*:

"One who abides in his own duty through right knowledge should not abandon those who possess knowledge; at that very moment, the knower is purified, while the ignorant one shall partake of what has been declared."

It has already been stated that even for those who follow worldly customs, there is no *sūtaka* (impurity) for those who eat separately from the cooked food and have been initiated into *nirvāṇa*. As it says in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:

Yogis should not abandon their practice even during periods of birth or death impurity.

"From anger, from hunger, from poison, from fire, or from the constant consumption of poison..."
From mountains and trees, there is loss of life within six months or a year.

For one who is devoid of ritual action, for the fool, for the coward, as well as for one burdened by debt and for the hypocrite,

There is no impurity regarding articles that have been specifically intended [for a rite]. Likewise, it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"In all cases of prosperity-rites (*vṛddhi*) or death-impurity (*śāva*), there is no *sūtaka* (birth-impurity)."
One should cause acts such as giving and worship to be performed with substances that have been mentally resolved.

Gold, a goat, a cow, sesame seeds, pure clarified butter, sesame, sugarcane, vegetables, salt, and wood;
Water, curd, ghee, oil, medicine, milk,

On the day of a son’s birth, there is no impurity regarding material goods, because it is a meritorious day due to the presence of the deities; as it is stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"When a son is born to those of the twice-born nature, both the gods and the ancestors arrive."
Therefore, on that day, it is always complete in every respect.
Therein, one should give gold, land, a cow, and likewise a horse; as well as an umbrella, a bull, clothing, garlands, a bed, a seat, and a house.
In that regard, there is also the authority for him to accept the funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍa*); and the father has the authority to give them. As it was stated by Trilocācārya:
"At birth, the navel-cord is not [severed]; prior to the giving [of the *piṇḍas*], the father possesses the fitness [to perform the rite]."

Impurity (*āśauca*) pertains to the village as well. Immediately after going outside [the village] to see a corpse, one must perform the worship of Śiva and other rites. This is stated in the *Kāraṇa*: "If a death occurs within the village during the twelve *daṇḍas* [of impurity], having abandoned..."
Having worshipped Śiva, one should perform the obligatory and occasional rites.

"One should perform the worship of Śiva when a person has died outside the village. This means that if one dies while situated within a street at a distance of eleven *dhanus* from the village boundary, the worship of Śiva and other rites must be performed in the other streets. Regarding this, Manu says:
One should not eat within a village where a corpse lies, nor study, nor offer oblations;
one should perform those acts at a distance of eleven bow-lengths from the edge of the road.
One must certainly perform the scriptural rites such as the *agnihotra* even when there is a corpse within [the village].
For when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti regarding another matter, Śruti alone is more authoritative.
Therefore, it is said: "One should offer the Śrauta fire in a village where a corpse is present."
In hamlets, towns, market towns, and royal capitals, there is indeed no fault regarding a corpse within [the settlement].
Thus says the Smṛti:
"In a hamlet, a town, a market town, and royal capitals, worship is performed through ritual action alone."
If one should perform it, the aforementioned fault does not exist.
Thus, the nature of the *kaṭikā* and other such places has been described in the *Suprabheda*. That which belongs to Brahmins or those of the same caste is known as a *sogrāma*;
that which is inhabited by Śūdras is proclaimed as a *kheṭaka*.
Within their boundaries, the dwelling of those who reside there is called a *kuṭika*; it is filled with the fourfold army and crowded with the king’s servants.
A royal residence is designated as a capital city when it is provided with goods from other regions for the purposes of buying and selling.
A *pattana* (port city) is on the shore of the ocean, while a *kharvaṭa* (market town) is at the end of those two.

Furthermore, this rule of ten days begins from the day of cremation for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*); for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), it begins from the day of death.

This is stated in the *Kāmika*: [The text continues: "In a village, [the period is] five days; in a town, six; in a city, seven; and in a capital city, eight. In a port city, nine days; and at the end of those, a market town is ten days. And this rule of ten days begins from the day of cremation for one who has maintained the sacred fires; for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, it begins from the day of death. This is stated in the *Kāmika*: [text follows].
The rites for one who has died, such as cremation and so forth, are performed once the duties have been completed;
for one who did not maintain the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), the period of impurity is declared to begin from the time of death.
The commencement [of the period of impurity] should be observed by relying on the emergence of the first day of the impurity.
As it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"When women experience the onset of menstruation at night, or when birth or death occurs, the first day [of the impurity] is indeed [the preceding day]."
The object of perception does not arise as long as the sun has not risen.

If a birth-impurity occurs during the midst of a birth-impurity, or a death-impurity occurs during the midst of a death-impurity, the purification of the latter is achieved by the former alone. Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
"O best of the twice-born, even if another birth-impurity should occur during a birth-impurity, [the purification is] by the first alone."
In the case of a death-impurity, purification occurs through another death-impurity.
And in the *Suprabheda*:
"Whether it be a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or even a death-impurity (*pretaka*), every day of the newly arrived impurity is nullified by the preceding impurity."
And in the *Candrajñāna*:
"Birth-impurity is purified by birth [recitation] alone; death-impurity is purified by death [recitation]."

If a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs during the period of impurity from a death (*śāva*), the death-impurity is extinguished by the birth-impurity. If a death-impurity occurs during the period of birth-impurity, the death-impurity is extinguished by the birth-impurity.
As it is stated in the *Candrajñāna* and *Kāmika* Tantras:

"When impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca) has arisen and impurity due to birth (sūtaka) occurs, one is purified by the death-impurity; birth-impurity does not purify death-impurity. Also in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"An increase [in merit] is not purified by death-impurity, nor is a corpse purified by an increase."

A short period of impurity (*alpāśauca*) is nullified by a long period of impurity (*dīrghāśauca*). However, if a long period of impurity occurs during the midst of a short period of impurity, it is not nullified. As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"If there should be a death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) within a death-impurity, or likewise a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) within a birth-impurity, [the latter] is [nullified] by the longer one."
There shall be purification, but one is not pure by means of fewer days.

If another period of impurity (āśauca) arises on the final day of a previous one, then an impurity of two days must be observed starting from the day after the end of the previous impurity. If it occurs on that very final day, then an impurity of three days is to be observed thereafter. Thus it has been said:
In the *Candrajñāna*, it is stated that if [the impurity] were purified after two days on the final day of the previous period,
then in the morning it would have been three days; thus, for sapindas, beyond ten days, this is the impurity of the elapsed ten-day period when heard within the middle of the three-month interval.
It should be performed for three nights; beyond that, up to the end of the year, it should be performed for one day upon hearing [the relevant passage].
Beyond this, bathing alone [is prescribed]; as it is stated in the Kāmika:
"If ten days have elapsed, one shall remain impure for three nights; in the Trika system, it shall be for that single day; and beyond a year, bathing alone [is required]."
And in the Kūrma Purāṇa it is stated:
"Regarding those who have passed away more than ten years ago, the impurity for sapindas lasts three nights; likewise, there is bathing upon death after the completion of one year."

In the case of those subject to impurity for three days or one day, when the period of impurity has passed, the purification occurs immediately or after one day respectively. For those subject to impurity for two days and a half (pakṣiṇī), if they hear of it within ten days, purification occurs at once; if they hear of it after ten days, purification occurs merely by bathing.

In the case of impurity due to birth (*sūtaka*) or death (*maraṇa*), the impurity lasts for one day immediately; for those who have undergone the *adhiṣvadhā* rite, it lasts for three days (*pakṣiṇī*); and otherwise, the time is until the pouring of the oblation (*srūk-seka*). Thus, if the news of a death is heard within the ten-day period of impurity, the learned hold that the impurity for all *sapiṇḍas* lasts only for the remainder of that period.
It is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"Even for those remaining among all [the deceased], this is the state of knowledge...
upon hearing of the death of one's mother or father before the collection of bones has taken place."
For a son, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts ten days from the day of the cremation;
this is also summarized [in the *Saṃgraha*]: "Before the collection of the bones for a son, it is ten days, and after that, it is eight.
Beyond ten days, it is as in the case of one year or more.

Regarding the ten-day period for the funeral rites (*daśāhika-aurdhvadehika*) performed upon the death of one's mother or father, it is said that [the impurity] belongs to the mother. Upon the death of the co-wife, their impurity lasts for ten days. Beyond one year, if the funeral rites have not been performed, there is a ten-day impurity in the case of the death of one's mother or father as heard in the tradition.
In the case of a stepmother, [the impurity lasts] for three days.
365) However, when the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) have been performed for one's mother or father, the impurity for that person lasts for three days, ending at the conclusion of the day.
In the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:
"If both parents should die, even if the son is far away, upon hearing the news,
impurity (*sūtaka*) shall last for ten days starting from that very day."
O best of the twice-born, the funeral rites for one's father’s wife who has passed away should be performed according to the prescribed rules, just as those for a mother.
Even when a year has passed, one remains impure for three nights.
This is clearly stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"In the case of hearing of the death of one's parents while they are absent, [the impurity lasts] ten nights; [if it is] after three days..."
In the case of both a mother and a co-wife, [the impurity lasts] ten days if it occurs within a year.

When the funeral rites (*dehika*) have been performed, there is one day of impurity for her, and three days for those two [the parents]. Here, even regarding the impurities caused by birth and death, there is a suspension of Vedic study and ritual acts for those who perform them.
On this point, Marīci says:
During the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), the abandonment of ritual acts such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*) and others is prescribed.

As stated in another *Smṛti*: "In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), for the four [classes] beginning with the *samaya*, there are respectively one, two, three, and four days of non-study (*anadhyāya*). Likewise, regarding giving (*dāna*): [the same applies].
Giving gifts, receiving them, burnt offerings, Vedic recitation, worship of the deities, and all rites such as the Vaiśvadeva are suspended during the period of birth-impurity.

Fearless toward the primordial deities—thus it is said in the Mataṅga: "O observer of good vows, supreme knowledge of the cause is not to be studied during auspicious times (*puṇyakāla*) nor during lunar phases (*nādotpatti*).

In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), for the four classes beginning with the *samaya*, the days of non-study (*anadhyāya*) are respectively one, two, three, and four days—as stated in that very same source:
"One, two, three, and four; and two for the *nāna*, *anta*, and *vastu* [sections] must be observed."
And [the procedure] for the consecration of the teacher and the sacrificer is as follows.
Immediate purification is prescribed for mortal attendants engaged in vows such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, or in activities such as the recitation of the Vedas (Pārāyaṇa) while making offerings of gold.
"In the case of a śrāddha or a pilgrimage to a sacred site, it may be done immediately;
likewise for those whose livelihood depends on [the recitation of] the Vedas, it should be given according to the sequence."
For four [types of] births, the days of non-study shall increase by one respectively; even during impurity (*sūtaka*), the worship of Śiva and Īśvara must be performed. As stated in the *Aṃśumat*:
"The neglect of progeny must not be committed during birth-impurity or death-impurity; it must be performed with the mantra of Śiva."
One becomes pure by merely bathing.
In that case, there shall be no impurity (aśauca), just as a lotus leaf remains unstained by water;
and in the Mataṅga:
"There is never an interruption of rites for the gods, the fire, or the guru."
Also in the Kālottara:
"He who, out of negligence, eats without having first worshipped the Supreme Lord— whether once, three times, four times, or even more— "
An expiation must be performed; otherwise, one shall go to hell. Even during periods of birth-impurity or death-impurity, the performance of worship must not be neglected.
p.
366) Therefore, one should always worship the *liṅga*, which is like a water bubble;
for he who eats without having worshipped it in due order is born even from the semen of a goat.
If one eats food that has not been offered, the giver partakes of misfortune.
Likewise, in the Skanda [Purāṇa]:
"O Śambhu, he who eats without having performed the worship of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) eats nothing but the five cruel impurities; of this there is no doubt."
And in the Brahmakaivarta [Purāṇa]:
"Food eaten by one who has omitted the worship of Īśāna is called impure plaything; they declare it to be a corpse.
That sinner, excluded by all people, goes to a terrible hell for an aeon."
In the Śivadharmottara:
"Even when in distress, a wise man who has worshipped Mahādeva would rather give up his life or even suffer the severing of his head."
One should not eat without first worshipping the three-eyed Lord; thus, he who performs the worship of Śiva for as long as he lives succeeds in his purpose.

Bound by human skin, he is indeed Rudra; of this there is no doubt. This worship of Śiva should be performed externally by those possessing excellence in devotion, knowledge, or dispassion; however, for those devoid of these, it should be performed internally. As stated in the Kāmika:
Whether it be devotion, knowledge, or detachment— or even any one of these— for whomsoever [these exist], the worship of the Samayin must be performed immediately.
"Even for one in whom these three [faculties] are dull or even very dull, the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) must be performed by means of praise. — *Aṃśumatī*, p.
It has been stated that for one performing the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the worship of the *liṅga* should be performed by a guru— whether of his own caste or another—
just as follows: "The ash, which is produced from the performance of one's own duties and is devoid of people, is mental (*mānasa*)."
The wise one should perform the dedication of all his gifts as a sacrifice.
Having worshipped the talliṅga, one should perform the worship with this very [mantra] alone, and not with a guru of one's own caste;
at the end, one should offer three handfuls of flowers.
At the end of the period of impurity, one should perform the rites according to the previous procedure;

thereafter, having offered a handful of flowers and mentally performed the recitation of the *ṛc*, the fire should be brought forth and established right there. Upon this, the worship within the pavilion for entry should be performed.
Because of his fitness, he should firmly perform worship solely for his own sake. As it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
"One should always worship for one's own sake; there is no impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*pretaka*)."
One should not perform worship for the sake of another by causing them to do so constantly.
One should always perform one's own duties, and never indeed the rites for the gods; for it is said in the *Aṃśumatī*:
"Knowing this, Sadāśiva always worships with effort during periods of birth-impurity, death-impurity, and ritual purification."
And especially for one's own sake.

Even for one who avoids food cooked by others (*sūtaka*), eats separately, and is initiated into *nirvāṇa*, the worship of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) must be performed with conceptualization (*vikalpa*). As it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "If one eats separately, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, this procedure is prescribed."
In this world, one may abandon [worldly life] for the sake of another or for the sake of concealment;
however, there is no abandonment of his recitation, circumambulation, and so forth. It is stated in the *Kālottara*:
Recitations, circumambulations, and other such rites must be performed with great effort.
For all those who are in a state of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), there is a fault in entering the outer enclosure.
As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
The introduction of all these various types [of deities] outside the main pavilion does not result in any fault.
Thus, the specific rules for those who have been initiated and are under ritual impurity (*āśauca*) are shown in that very same [text],
as follows:
"The three castes (*varṇa*) who are under impurity must enter the inner pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) at intervals."
O Lord of Sages, this shall certainly not be a fault for those who have been initiated.
But when others enter after that, one should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
outside of that boundary, their entry does not result in any fault.
Thus [it is said] regarding the touching of cows by those in a state of birth-impurity (sūtakin) or those handling the dead (pretakin).
One must indeed abandon even those flowers that have been touched by the light [of the impurity] of such flowers;
as it is stated in the *Kālottara*: "Upon contact with a flower belonging to one in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), one should discard the flower-vessels with the Aghora-weapon mantra."
One should perform one hundred thousand fire-oblations with the mantra.
There is a fault in touching [the beads] during impurity (*sūtaka*), and likewise when there is a *lakṣa* [of other defects].
In the *Skandakālottara*, the wearing of Rudrākṣas is forbidden for a woman, unless she is endowed with the purificatory rite of initiation (*dīkṣā-saṃskāra*). During *sūtaka*...
"One should never wear a rudrākṣa during a death-impurity (mṛtaka),
nor should one who is menstruating or even one touched by a caṇḍāla wear it. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmakaivarta* as well.
Some maintain that one is purified from birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), death-impurity (*śava*), the voiding of water or excrement, and contact with a woman by wearing *akṣamālā* (rosaries) and the like;
according to the view of some, for the destruction of one's own life-force, [one should wear] at the neck or on the arms [rosaries] of the elements accompanied by mantras.
Regarding rudrākṣas, there is no prohibition for a large rosary; indeed, only the large one is excluded.

As it is stated in that very same work: "Others have always declared that wearing [rudrākṣas] on the arm or neck removes sin; however, a large rosary should not be worn [on these parts], even when preceded by mantra."

Regarding the word "in purity": for a noble woman who is menstruating, if menstrual flow appears again after twenty days have passed, her impurity lasts for three nights. As it is stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:
"A woman who is already menstruating becomes menstruating once again..."
After twenty days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights.
