In the *Suprabheda*, however, a specific purification is shown for each of the three days as well.
It is as follows:
On the first day she is a Caṇḍālī; on the second, a slayer of Brahmins; on the third, she is called a washerwoman;
on the fourth day, she becomes pure.

And for her, during those three days, bathing and other such acts must be avoided; she should eat only once a day, using only her cupped hands, and drink water from a vessel— thus it is stated in that very same source.

For three nights, she remains untainted by menstrual flow, abstaining from bathing and other such rites; eating but one meal a day, she shall not drink water from a vessel, but only from her cupped hands.

Thus, on the fourth day, having performed a bath preceded by the cleansing of the teeth (dantadhāvana) and having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or clarified butter (ghṛta), one should worship Śiva; this applies also to the preceding three days.
The worship of Śiva must be performed at the end [of the day]; likewise, it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:

"Having purified the teeth and other impurities with clay, one should bathe repeatedly; then, having consumed either the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) or clarified butter, one should worship Śiva."
The internal sacrifice (antaryāga) should be performed during the three days preceding that [day].

When performing the internal sacrifice on the fourth day, one should recite the Aghora mantra a thousand times, consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and worship Śiva. As stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:

Alternatively, one should recite the Ghoramantra a thousand times at the end. Regarding this, specific rules for purification in the event of mutual contact among menstruating women— whether they be of the same caste or of different castes— have been set forth by Parāśara as follows:
If two women of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya castes, while in their menses, touch one another,
the former shall perform half a *kṛcchra* penance, and the latter likewise one quarter.
If a Brāhmaṇī woman and a Śūdra-born woman touch each other while in their menses,
the former is purified by the Kṛcchra penance, while the Śūdra woman is purified by bathing.
Vyāsa: When two women who are menstruating— belonging to the same lineage and having the same husband— touch one another, whether intentionally or unintentionally, they become pure by bathing.

Upon touching a woman in her menses— whether intentionally, unintentionally, or through doubt— one should perform, respectively, one thousand, five hundred, or one hundred and eight recitations of the mantra of the Lord of one's own caste during the worship of Śiva. In the case of touching a woman of a lower caste who is in her menses, [the same applies] for one of lower status.
The recitation [of mantras] should be performed for half the number previously mentioned; as it is stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya* (p.
"If one worships Śiva with a desire [for results] while touched by a woman of one's own caste who is in her courses..."
Then, one should recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family (Sajatīśvara) one thousand times.
If one worships him out of ignorance, one becomes pure for that purpose;
if a doubt arises, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
"In contact with one of lower caste, the penance increases progressively by two, three, and four times; in contact with one of superior caste, the inferior person shall perform half of that.
Thus, the distinction between those who act with desire and those who do not is demonstrated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
As it is said:
"Due to fate, disease, delusion, fear of kings, thieves, and so forth—through these defects there is lack of desire; the remainder should be understood as being due to desire."
Upon touching water that has been touched by a menstruating woman, purification occurs through bathing;
for it is said that one who has touched water touched by a woman in her courses (udakyā) and others becomes pure after performing a bath.
Now, since women have as their sole duty the service of their husbands, they lack independence.

If it is asked, "How can there be an application to the worship of Śiva through initiation (dīkṣā) by virtue of its being a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) that confers qualification?"— it is not so; for those [rites] demonstrate the qualification for the purification of Śiva through the permission granted by the Lord and others.
A noble woman has no independent entitlement to the rites of Śiva-consecration;
she is entitled only through her connection with her husband, provided she is endowed with devotion to the Lord.
In the same way, for a woman deprived of her husband, there is indeed the authority [to perform rites] with the permission of her son and wife;
and for a maiden, there is authority with the permission of her father.
At the conclusion of the section on impurity caused by birth and death, which has been set forth in the subsequent passage,
the ritual bath at the time of conception and the touching of water must be performed by a Brāhmaṇa alone.

A Kṣatriya must perform a ritual bath and touch a vehicle and so forth; Vaiśyas must also perform a ritual bath and touch *vṛtauda* (boiled rice); and a Śūdra must also perform a ritual bath and touch a staff. As stated in the *Uttarasaṃgraha*:
"Having bathed at the end of the *agha* [impurity] during a great sacrifice (*sumakha*), one who has been touched by a Brahmin becomes pure.

Regarding kings and others, as well as vehicles and so forth, Manu spoke otherwise. In this matter, there are external Smṛti rules; however, for initiated Śaivas, it must be performed at the end of the *agha*.

There is a distinction. It is stated that for those such as *putrakas* who have performed either an internal (*antaryāga*) or external (*bahiryāga*) sacrifice during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), they must— upon the end of the impurity— perform a ritual bath, eat only at night for one day, recite the *Aghora* mantra a thousand times, and perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part of that number.
In the case of a combination [of circumstances]:

for those observing impurity who are *samayins*, the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsti*) is to be performed without mantras; there should be no touching of the *liṅga*, but internal worship of Śiva must be performed.
For the wise who are endowed with devotion and dispassion, whose minds are fixed on the worship of the Liṅga, and who abide by their observances, there is no impurity at the time of worship.
At the conclusion of that, he should perform eating only at night for one day, a thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra,
and a pair consisting of bathing in the Gaḍḍuka and the fire-oblation (homa).

For those such as the *putraka* who have abandoned the worship of Śiva due to their connection with a death or birth impurity (*pretaka-sūtaka*), from the day the impurity begins until its conclusion, they must perform a fast at night preceded by bathing three times a day, worship, the recitation (*japa*) of the *Ghorasahasra* mantra a thousand times, and the fire sacrifice (*agnihoma*).
And one should eat only as much food as is necessary;
as it says in that very same [text] on page 373:
For one who performs daily rites on the anniversary of the birth of a deceased person,
there is impurity for as many days as the period of ritual defilement (āśauca) lasted for that individual.

Preceded by bathing at the three periods of the day, worship, fire-rituals, recitation, and burnt offerings, the rite should be performed with a thousand repetitions of the *ghora* mantra until the evening meal.
Even cremation makes a person pure; likewise, it is stated in another Smṛti:

"Regarding the occasion of impurity due to death, there are two [purifications]: killing and dying. For kinsmen, purity comes from the death [of the deceased] itself, but for the cremator, it comes from the cremation."
In this case, even for one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* but is the cremator, there occurs impurity due to death (*maraṇāśauca*),

because both [the impurity of] death and cremation are equal in being caused by the fact of death. Since this impurity of cremation is more powerful than the impurity of death, it causes that [death-impurity] to cease.
It does not exist—thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
"The impurity of death is twice that of birth; the impurity of menstruation is twice that of death;
the impurity of birth is twice that of menstruation; and the cremation [impurity] is twice even that."
Impurity due to cremation, when occurring apart from impurity due to the cremation of a father, is extinguished during the midst of the impurity caused by cremation;

for both are equal, owing to their having an identical number of days and a common cause. As it is stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*: "In the case of a coincidence of two impurities of equal duration, one is purified [by the end of that period]."
Regarding "equally": that burning is of two kinds. First, there is the initial burning, and then there is the subsequent burning.
The burning of what has been directly practiced is the initial burning.

In this case, there is no inequality regarding the impurity (āśauca) of the sapinda relatives; rather, there is cremation or re-cremation according to the physical form [of the remains]. It is stated in the Smṛti:
"Or, by means of a heap of asna-palāśa leaves, one should fashion a representative image on the path."
Having washed the bones with milk, one should cremate them like a *preta*.
The cremation of the physical form is also described in the *Suprabheda*:
"The death of one who has spoken [the mantra] occurs by means of a weapon from the beginning of the sequence;
[otherwise], there are causes for self-destruction such as smallpox, consumption, leprosy, and the like."
The physical appearance of those who die by water, or even by horned animals, or especially by fire, is now described.
When [the breath] has gone to another region by means of the serpent, the animal, or the elephant, and has transcended the limit of the twelve [fingers],
the burning of the form is prescribed.
In cases where death by weapons or other such means occurs after one year has passed, one should cremate the body without mantras or bury it in the ground.
Having covered it with *sudarbha* grass and bound it with thread, one should fashion the form;
then, having wrapped it with *plāśa* leaves, one should indeed secure it with thread.
"A wise person should cause all the rites for one whose child has died to be performed;
the cremation of the image is thus prescribed. However, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated that the making of the image should be done with kusha grass, flour, or clay, as follows:
For one who has perished in another country, one should fashion an image of him out of clay from that region,
or an image made of kuśa grass, or one produced from cow dung.
"One should cause the inner liṅga to be bathed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)," so it is said in the *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*.

For one who has died in another country, as well as for an initiated person (dīkṣita) who has died, the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi) should be performed even with kuśa grass, having first fashioned a physical likeness (prakṛti) of the deceased.
And in the Kūrma [Purāṇa]:
"In the absence of the body, an effigy made of Palāśa leaves should then be cremated by the sapindas, endowed with faith, according to the proper rule."

Furthermore, regarding those who have died an untimely death (*durmṛta*), it is stated therein that for the purpose of removing their state as a *piśāca*— which exists among the eight classes of birth within the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*)— there should be a cremation of the physical form preceded by a hundred thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra and an offering (*bali*) to Rudra. As it is said:
Now, for those whose lives were taken through negligence, or by thieves, snakes, fire, or elephants, tigers, the current of a river, or drowning in a grasper (crocodile).
Having extracted [the body] from those who have committed suicide or others who have killed themselves,
one should first burn their body silently with the Śiva-fire.

Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times, one should offer the Rudra-bali as prescribed; then, having bathed, sipped water, and returned, one should feed those whose wealth is austerity.
Having satisfied the eight bearers of the great vows, or those such as the Pāśupatas and others,
with garments and sacrificial fees, he should dismiss them.
Having fashioned a doll out of *darbha* grass as a counterpart to that body, and having performed the remainder of the rite as previously described, one should unite it with the stainless state.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Then, at the end of the year or after six months, having again performed the consecration (*saṃskāra*),
one should offer three nights of water and perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and other rites."

If a person who has gone to another country passes away after twelve years have elapsed, the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) for him should be performed preceded by the cremation of his physical form; furthermore, the widowhood of his wife must be observed. If, having been treated in this manner, the husband returns from that other country, then by him—

Prior to the wedding, an auspicious mark should be placed by the wife upon her neck with an upper garment (*uttarīya*). This is stated in the *Suprabheda*: "When one has gone from one country to another..."
When twelve years have passed, cremation is prescribed for the physical form; if his wife is present there, she should undergo the rites of widowhood in due order.
He performed other propitiatory rites (balikarma) along with the recitation of mantras; thereafter, when she had arrived, he likewise provided her with auspicious ornaments.
"One should fasten an auspicious upper garment around the neck of the wife.
Furthermore, the procedure for his remarriage is shown in the *Kālādarśa*;
however, in the *Kāmika*:

Regarding defects of the lunar day (*tithi*), weekday (*vāra*), and asterism (*nakṣatra*), as well as the occurrence of burning or death— for example: "O auspicious lady, when the asterism has three quarters and Venus, Mars, or Jupiter [are present], for those who undergo burning or death, it becomes the cause of the destruction of their lineage."
"For that very purpose, cremation should again be performed with care.
The auspicious [days] are the second, seventh, and twelfth lunar days; and the three-quarter constellations are Kṛttikā, Phalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Punarvasu, and Viśākhā.
The six stars of the Pūrvābhādrapadā nakṣatra; furthermore, in other Smṛtis, re-burning is prescribed for others as well.

Even for one who has been consecrated with mantras, if the water-libation ceremony (*udaka-kriyā*) has not been completed, re-incineration is prescribed after the lapse of ten days; thus [it is said]:
"For those cremated without prior mantras, there is the drying up of bodily defects through the power [of the ritual]."
And it is intended that there shall be a re-burning of those who have already died.

Furthermore, this cremation is of two kinds: internal (*ādhyātmika*) and external (*bāhyaka*). Regarding the first, there is impurity for all [relatives] for six days, as it is said in the *Saṃgraha*: "In the case of a second cremation, the learned say there is impurity for one day. External cremation is also of two kinds:

Regarding the cases of "re-burning of one who has already performed a sacrifice" (*yajvapunardahana*) and "re-burning of one who has not performed a sacrifice" (*ayajvapunardahana*): in the first case, there is a period of ten days, as stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:
"In the case of re-burning for one who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), even then it is for ten nights. In the second case, it is for three days.

As it is stated in that very same [text]: "In the case of cremation after a lapse of time, again for three days. However, in the *Saṃgraha*, regarding the cremation of bones, an alternative period of full impurity (*pūrṇa-tryahāśauca*) is mentioned, based on the option of whether or not the bones were collected before the collection of the ashes; as it says: "If the collection of the bones occurs first, as previously [stated]. This refers to the cremation of bones.

Furthermore, regarding cremation in all cases, it is as stated: "In that very case, for a son, a period of ten nights is desired here. Now, the following is stated concerning the pursuit, carrying out, and cremation of ordinary mortals; first, the pursuit of those belonging to the Śaiva [tradition].

We shall explain the distinction between the two types of carrying forth [the corpse] immediately hereafter. Regarding following [the funeral procession], however, on that very day one is unfit for ritual acts; purification occurs through bathing, touching fire, consuming clarified butter, bathing again, and breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
If one follows a member of the same caste, even if it is a person of a different caste, purification is attained by these means.
It is stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:
"If one follows a deceased person out of desire, whether they be a relative or even a stranger..."

"Having bathed with one's clothes on, touched fire, and consumed clarified butter (ghṛta), one becomes pure. For a Brahmin who follows a Śūdra [corpse], purification occurs after three days; for following the corpses of Vaiśyas or Kṣatriyas, it is two days.
For these [latter cases], purification is achieved through the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra more than a thousand times and bathing in a river.
Upon following a deceased person who is a Śūdra, a twice-born (dvija), or similar [low-caste] individual, purification is attained through bathing.
Upon following a deceased Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya, purification is attained through bathing, touching fire, and consuming ghee. For a Brāhmaṇa [following] a Vaiśya or a king...

In the case of following a deceased person of the *preta* state, purification is attained through bathing and the recitation of the *gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times, along with the performance of the *pakṣi-sāha* rite in due order. For a *śūdra* who follows a deceased *śūdra* or touches a corpse, the impurity lasts for one day; otherwise, it lasts for one meal-time (*ekakāla*). This is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
The twice-born are purified by bathing, touching fire, reciting the *jyāśa* [mantra], bathing again, and strict self-restraint,
even when following the corpse of one of their own caste.
For a Brahmin who follows a Śūdra for three days, [the penance is] two days [for following] a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya;
then there is bathing in a river and the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra one thousand and eight times.

A Śūdra is purified from contact with the dead among the twice-born by bathing; a merchant and a king by bathing, touching fire, and drinking water; and those who follow the corpse of their own kin by bathing, touching fire, and drinking water.

When a Brāhmaṇa follows the corpse of a Vaiśya or a king, there is a three-day period [of impurity], bathing in a river daily, and the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times. When following the corpse of a Śūdra, there is the Rudra-japa, touching the corpse, and likewise eating only once a day. However, in the *Prāyaścitta-samuccaya*, it is stated that for a Brāhmaṇa [following] a Kṣatriya...
In the case of following [the corpse], it lasts for one, two, or three days.
379) It has been stated that when a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya follows the corpse of a Śūdra, the period of impurity lasts for a day and a night (*pakṣiṇī*). As it is said:

Upon following a corpse of a Kṣatriya or others, one is purified in one, two, or three nights respectively; for having followed the corpse of a Śūdra, a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya is purified in one day or a pakṣiṇī [period], according to Manu.
And "carrying away" (nirharaṇa) consists of the forms of preparing the bier, carrying [the body], cremating it, and so forth.
When that carrying away has been performed, for those entitled to the three-day impurity who offer water, the impurity lasts for one day;
however, upon the death of one not yet initiated (*anupanīta*), for the *sapiṇḍas* entitled to the ten-day paternal impurity, it lasts for ten days.

For those related by marriage and for female birds who have become impure, the period of impurity lasts three days. However, for those of a different caste, the impurity is that which is prescribed according to the caste of the deceased. As stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"Impurity lasting ten days applies to kinsmen (*jñāti*) who offer water; for those related by marriage (*yoni-bandhu*), it lasts three nights."
It is stated that for one who has performed the removal of a corpse belonging to a different caste, [the following applies].

When the removal of a deceased person is performed for one who is unrelated by death and belongs only to the same caste (*sajātīya*), the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for one day and night, or until the sun is seen at night or the stars are seen during the day. Furthermore, there shall be residence outside the village and the touching of fire; [the purification is completed] with the *pañcagavya*.

And the consumption of one of the two portions of clarified butter must be performed. It is stated in the Kāmika: "The carrier who has touched the corpse should dwell outside the village until the appearance of the stars, or until the appearance of the sun."
Having touched the fire at the end [of the cremation], they should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) or clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Upon seeing the purpose of the removal of the corpse, even for those who are *sapiṇḍas*, the period of impurity for those of one's own caste becomes double. For those of the same caste, however, the impurity is that which is prescribed according to the specific caste of the deceased.
As Gautama has said:
"Having seen the object [of the gift] during the removal of a deceased person, one should give twice as much to the kinsmen, but it is inferior."
"But for those of different castes, the rule stated for the corpse of one's own caste applies."
In the case of the funeral rites for the Lord of Ascetics (yatīndra), there is immediate purification and the attainment of great fruit;
this has been stated in the *Saṃgraha*, as well as in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: [The text continues with the verses from those works.]
He who takes away a Śiva-yogin who has passed away— being without companion and without protector— and performs the funeral rites for him,
is joined with the most undesirable [consequences].
All this applies to ordinary mortals. As stated in the *Kāmika*: "This has been proclaimed as the general rule for human beings.
However, for Śaivas, when carrying or cremating the corpse of a deceased Śaiva who has received initiation (*dīkṣita*), [the rite is performed with] the *aghora* [mantra].
Purification is attained by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and twenty times. In the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:
"Those initiated for a *śivapreta* should perform twice the number of recitations;
so too should those who carry the corpse on their shoulders, even if they have offered it with faith."

When the rites such as bathing have been performed for deceased practitioners (*sādhaka*), teachers (*ācārya*), or their sons, purification is attained by bathing and reciting the *Saṃhitā* one hundred times. It is stated in the *Brahmaśambhu*:
"Having performed the rites such as the falling [of the body] for practitioners, teachers, and their sons, and having bathed, [one should recite] one hundred [times]."
Having recited the Saṃhitā, one should worship Śiva.
For those who follow [the funeral procession] and for those who have been initiated, purification comes from reciting the Aghora mantra one hundred times.
For those who carry the body, the cremator, and for the preceptors, it is the same: the Aghora mantra one hundred times.

Regarding the statement "purification comes from reciting [the mantra] twice": it is said in that very same source—having offered the funeral oblation (skandanda) or performed the cremation, and having bathed, one should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred times; likewise, for the funeral rites of the gurus, the disciples should recite it one hundred times.
The fruit of carrying the corpse of one who has been initiated is also stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Whoever carries a deceased Brāhmaṇa who has received Śiva-initiation, whether he was observing a vow or not,
shall not suffer an untimely death."
Alternatively, the word "or" (*vā*) should be construed with the term "Brāhmaṇa.

Thus, the meaning is that there is no such thing as an untimely death for one who carries the corpse of a deceased Brāhmaṇa—whether he be observing a vow or not—or for anyone else who has merely received Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣita*). [This applies even to] one devoid of initiation and inferior...

Purification is achieved by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times. As it is said in that very same work: "A person of lower caste who is devoted to a vow must not be followed by one of the highest caste; having followed him, one should bathe in water and recite the *svajātīśa* [mantra] one hundred times."

Those who have not been initiated (adīkṣita) must not touch the corpse of an initiated person (dīkṣita) among their sapinda relatives; as stated in that very [text]: "The uninitiated shall not touch the initiated, nor the initiated the uninitiated.
Due to touching the corpse of an uninitiated person, those who are initiated must bathe outside the village.
One should remain outside at night, observe the stars, wear [the prescribed] clothing, touch fire, consume clarified butter, recite two hundred *saṃhitās*, and fast during the day;
as it is stated in that very same source:
He who touches the corpse of one who has been initiated or one who has not been initiated must bathe outside the village and remain there until the appearance of the stars.
Having stayed there and bathed, one should touch [the deity] after consuming ghee;
then, having fasted, the initiate (samayin) should recite the Saṃhitā twice.
If there is contact with human bone that still has moisture, one should recite the Aghoraśata mantra.
If the contact is with something dry, one should perform a bath, look at the sun, and then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
As it is stated in that very same source:
Having touched a human corpse, one who possesses firm attachment [to worldly things] should bathe and recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times; if it was a corpse without attachment, he should bathe.

Upon touching something without oil (or fat), he should bathe or gaze at the sun while remaining silent. "Roda" is a term for the appearance of a sick person. [In the case] of touching a corpse, [the penance is] that which causes weeping; however, in the absence of that, [it is] free from such [weeping].
Prior to the collection of the bones (*asthisañcayana*), there is a single period [of impurity]; after that, there is only bathing.
However, for a king (*nṛpa*) and a Vaiśya, upon the death of someone of their own caste, prior to the collection of the bones, there is bathing with one's clothes on;
after that, there is merely bathing. But for a Brāhmaṇa, upon the death of someone of his own caste... [the rule is as follows].

Before the collection of the bones (sañcayana), there is bathing; after that, there is sipping water (ācamana). When a superior person dies, for a person of lower status, there is one day of impurity before the collection of the bones, and bathing thereafter. For a king or a Vaiśya, when a Śūdra dies, there are two days of impurity before the collection of the bones, and one day thereafter.
For a Brāhmaṇa, [the impurity lasts] three days prior to the collection of the bones (*sañcayana*) when a Śūdra dies; after that, it is one day.
As stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"Likewise, there is only bathing upon the death of a Śūdra; upon the collection of the bones, there is bathing for one who has touched the bones of those of his own caste."
For a king and a vaiśya who have accumulated [impurity], bathing with one's clothes on is prescribed; for a brāhmaṇa, sipping water (ācamana) and bathing suffice.

For those of lower status, bathing and sipping water are required after performing the sacrifice (iṣṭi); however, for the foremost of the castes, bathing for a full day is required. Previously... [p. 383]
Afterwards, the patient and the attendant should remain alone on a bed of bones.

When the collection of bones has not yet been performed, for a Śūdra it is two days; when the donor's caste marks have been removed, for a twice-born it is three days, and for a Brāhmaṇa it is one day, provided the collection [of the body] has already taken place.
In this regard, concerning the characteristics of the deceased, the specific statements of Kūrma should be consulted, as follows:
"If a Śūdra whose bones have not yet been gathered should cry out while a Brāhmaṇa is present, [the impurity lasts] for three nights."
In that case, the period of impurity would last for one day; otherwise, it would be different.

For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, there is one day of impurity prior to the collection of the bones; otherwise, it is immediate. But for those who reside in the state of Brahman, it is indeed immediate.
"If a Brahmin who has accumulated bones dies, then purification occurs by bathing with one's clothes on;
of this there is no doubt.
Thus, the consumption of food for the deceased (*pretānna*) is of two kinds: intentional and unintentional. Regarding that—
In cases of intentional [impurity], impurity persists until its cessation;

upon that cessation, purification is achieved through bathing. During times of famine and the like, one must observe impurity for the duration of the meal-day and perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*). As stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
If one eats their food even once intentionally, then, upon the cessation of that period of impurity,
he becomes pure by bathing; however,
if a man eats it until the end because of famine, [he remains impure].
"For as many days as [the food remained], there is impurity; thereafter, one should perform penance.
384) In the case of unintentional consumption, the period of impurity lasts until the food has been digested. As it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:

"Until what has been eaten is digested, it falls away. Regarding this, the expiation consists of drinking cow's milk ten times and performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. It is stated in the Svāyambhuva [Smṛti]: "The food of one in a state of impurity due to death, the food at the end of a birth-impurity, and likewise the food at the Sīmantonnayana ceremony..."

"Having consumed [it] ten times with cow's milk, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. The nature of the Cāndrāyaṇa is to be seen in the *Kiraṇa*. However, in the *Kālottara*, the expiation is stated:
"If it has been consumed during a period of impurity (*sūtaka*), or during the increase of impurity (*sūtavṛddhi*)," and so forth.
One should recite the terrible mantra one thousand times out of desire.
Furthermore, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, the expiation for various kinds of food, such as that from a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and so forth, is stated as follows:
Having eaten at an Abdamaṅgala rite, for a male child, or likewise at the Sīmantonnayana ceremony, or during the birth-impurity (sūtaka),
one should recite the Ghoramantra one thousand times.
One should recite the hundred [verses] during the naming ceremony, the birth-rite, as well as the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, the initiation vow, the gift of the cow, and the marriage.
Having eaten that food on the fourth day, one should recite it a thousand times; at a *pākayajña*, a *haviyajña*, or a *somayāga*, one should recite it a hundred times.
He who, having consumed the food of one who has departed on a journey for a period of up to a year,
should begin the *sadyaḥ-śrāddha* and mutter ten thousand recitations of the *Dakṣiṇā*.
In the case of an *ekoddiṣṭa* or a *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, [the recitation] should be a thousand times;
or rather, when one eats at a *sadyaḥśrāddha*, no fault is found therein.
He who eats at the prescribed times, having bathed after digestion as previously described, [attains the fruit].
Having thus performed the expiation, one should worship the Lord and not otherwise.

"Contact with those below" (adhassamparka) refers to sitting, sleeping, or eating in the same row together with them and so forth. When that has occurred, impurity (āśauca) lasts for as many days as the duration of the contact.
As stated in the *Kūrma-purāṇa*:
"He who shares a seat with them, or even engages in sleeping and so forth, whether he be a kinsman or a non-kinsman,
becomes pure after ten days."

Herein is the rule regarding the ten-day period; it concerns the subject of contact for ten days. Since other Smṛtis have not specified the number of days of contact as the duration of impurity, it is stated in the Saṃgraha: "Impurity resulting from contact shall last for the number of days [of that contact]. This...

Impurity arising from contact pertains to women only in relation to property and ritual acts; as it is stated in that very same work: "But for women, impurity arising from contact does not apply to property and ritual acts.
Regarding impurity other than that arising from contact, one who is subject to that impurity...

Because of the impurity of the substance, when that substance is used in the worship of deities and similar rites, bathing, pacification (*śānti*), *homa*, and other such rituals must be performed. This is stated in the *Candrajñāna*:
"If one who knows the mantras should employ a substance associated with impurity, then let [the following be done]..."
The bathing of the deities for worship, and the performance of peace-offering oblations.
Thereafter, one should cause pure food, accompanied by parched grain, to be offered, together with the sounding of conch shells and filled with the noise of musical instruments.

In this context, regarding impurity due to death (*mṛtaka-āśauca*), one must perform the touching of the body for as many days as the period of impurity lasts. Regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), on that day, there is bathing upon touching someone who is not subject to impurity.
One who touches a person in a state of impurity (*āśauca*) must perform a *kṛcchra* penance. As stated in that very same source:
"One should avoid touching the limbs [of one] within the ten-day period [of birth];
for four days after a birth, however, the Smṛti declares that bathing removes the impurity of touching such a person."
In the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*, bathing upon contact with those who have touched a corpse and others is prescribed:

"One who has touched a corpse, one who has carried out the dead, one who has gone to a cremation ground, or one who has touched those in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*prata*), becomes pure only through bathing after being touched by those who have delivered a child or those who have performed the cremation."
Regarding contact with a menstruating woman, three baths are prescribed; as it is said in that very same source:

"Upon touching the body of a menstruating woman, one should then perform three baths. However, for a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), seeing her or speaking with her is prohibited until ten days have passed, as follows:

In that case, regarding the combination [of impurities], for a male birth there shall be ten nights of impurity characterized by the mother's inability to see and so forth, and twenty-two nights characterized by the suspension of *śrāddha* rites; for a female birth, it shall be ten nights more than that. [Furthermore,] one may touch those subject to impurity without using raw food (*āma*).

There is the relinquishing of substances. Regarding the eating of food from a vessel touched by such [impurity], purification occurs by drinking water with *kuśa* grass, *udumbara* wood, and *kathi* grass. It is stated in the Smṛti:
"Upon contact with substances, one should discard everything along with the earth; having eaten..."
It is unfit for consumption if it is defiled by impurities, insects, or hair.
One is purified even by drinking a decoction made from kuśa grass, udumbara, bilva, and others, as well as panasa, lotus leaves, śaṅkhapuṣpī, suvarcā, and so forth.
Even the failure to perform the tonsure ceremony prescribed for birth and death brings about a person’s unfitness for ritual action.
As it is stated in the Smṛti: "He whose hair has grown on his head but has not been shorn on the tenth day..."

"In that case, the impurity (āśauca) would dissolve; therefore, one should have the hair shaved. Shaving is prescribed for the father on the tenth day following a birth, but on the first day following a death.
Furthermore, shaving is prescribed for all the immediate descendants (anubhāvinaḥ) as well on the tenth day.
A specific shaving (vapanaviśeṣa) is prescribed; if those [specific acts] are not performed, their impurity (āśauca) does not cease.
In the event of a prohibition against shaving, there is no fault for them regarding food. Among these, shaving is prohibited for one who is pregnant, as stated in the Svāyambhuva [Smṛti].
Following a dog, shaving the head, and bathing in the Indus— by performing these while pregnant, a husband will certainly become childless.
In the *Smṛti* as well: "Shaving, following [the corpse], clipping the nails, performing a *śrāddha*, building a house,
traveling a long distance, marriage, and touching the waters of the ocean."

"The application [of the ritual] results in the exhaustion of the lifespan for those who have entered the womb. During the initiation of the ancestors (*pitṛ-dīkṣā*), the shaving of the hair (*vapana*) for one's kin must not be performed. As it is said in that very same source:
"They should perform the initiation of the ancestors, but they should not cause the hair-shaving of their caste-kin (*jāti-kṣaura*)."
When two wives are both pregnant, the shaving of the head should not be performed for one who is carrying a male child.
As it is said in that very same source:
"If a woman with two husbands is pregnant, and the other wife has recently given birth, there should be no shaving at all."
One should perform the naming ceremonies, or have them performed.
Upon the death of one's mother or others, or when there is a pregnancy, a shaving of the head must be performed.
As it is said in that very same [text], p. 387b):

One should cause [the seed] to be sown even by one who is pregnant in the case of the mother, the father, the preceptor, the maternal uncle, the elder brother, the sister's husband, the father-in-law, and the teacher’s wife.

In the case of a mother’s initiation (*dīkṣā*), if the father dies, there is cremation alone; in the case of a father’s initiation, if the mother dies, both cremation and shaving take place. As it is said in that very same [text]:
"But if the father dies before the mother’s initiation, there shall be cremation for the fathers; but for the father..."

"In the previous initiation, burning and shaving [of the hair] are performed in sequence. Regarding cremation at night, having omitted the shaving and performed the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), the shaving should be performed on the following day. Thus says Kātyāyana:
If [the body] is cremated at night, one should perform the rites up to the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), excluding the shaving;
on the following day, the shaving is prescribed there, involving only the hair.
Even the non-performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* renders the primary performer unfit for ritual acts. As it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"The primary performer remains impure until the liberation of the deceased. [This refers to] the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

This is the liberation from the state of a preta. Among the various rites for pretas, there are five: the cremation of the body, the placement of stones, the taking of water, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and the single-offering (ekoddiṣṭa) śrāddha performed on the day of death, consisting of covering the naked, providing food for the elderly, and the fire-śrāddha.

The *śrāddhas*, the water-pots (*sotakuṃbha*), and the *śrāddha* rites preceded by those [preparations]—among these, the *piṇḍīkaraṇa* belongs primarily to the principal [deceased]; however, the other [rites] belong to the principal as well. In that regard, for those who perform the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) for those whose [caste] signs (*aliṅga*) and species (*jāti*) have been purified according to the proper time and other requirements...
"In the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one is primary.
388) In the non-proximity of each preceding one, each subsequent one attains primacy.

The summary verse regarding their authors is as follows: [The author] is the son of Kriyā; from the three noble ladies [his mother, paternal grandmother, and maternal grandmother], his brothers, his mother, his daughter-in-law, his sister, and the wife of that [brother]; those who recite it [the lineage]; the sapinda-relatives; those entitled to the water-offering (udaka); the disciples and so forth; the bridegroom and the bride; the friend and the king—these are the [categories].

There are twenty-one [categories]. Regarding the previous [classification], it is said that "the one who performs the consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the deceased is the most excellent. In this context, the status of being the performer is stated to follow the sequence of son, brother, and so forth, starting with those without sons. Among these, primarily, there are five types of pure [performers].

[The rites] end with the *saṃskāras*, end with the *piṇḍadāna*, end with the *sañcayana*, end with the *ekoddiṣṭa*, and end with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Prior to the fourth [day], they end with the *saṃskāras*; in that context, since digging itself constitutes the *saṃskāra*, the offering of water is not required. As it is stated in the *Smṛti*:
"Or they burn the water-piṇḍa.

After that, until the end of the annual piṇḍa-offerings, [the rites] up to the eighth year consist of the collection of bones (*sañcayana*) ending with the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; beyond that, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* takes place. This is the non-primary [view].

For the performer, however, there are only four purifications; because he is ineligible for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, even his death results in purification only at the conclusion of the *ekoddiṣṭa*. As it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"He reaches the state of purified impurity only at the end of the *ekoddiṣṭa*. Here, [the rule is] general.

The investigation of mortals and the detailed exposition of rites such as the offering of water-clods and the *śrāddha* have been extensively elaborated upon in the *Smṛtis* and need not be further expanded here. However, regarding the *samayins*, *putrakas*, and *ācāryas* of the Śaivas, there is a potential transgression of their *samaya* (vow/obligation) if they are remembered elsewhere [in a manner inconsistent with their status].
The final rites for the preceptors must be performed by the disciple through the study and mastery of the Dharma, for the sake of attaining the state of Śiva.

Then, the rite of cremation (*saṃyojana-saṃskāra*) must be performed for the deceased body by means of the Śiva-fire. Thereafter, on that very same day, one should proceed in order with the covering of the corpse, the shaving [of the hair], and the preparation of either a bier or a funeral seat on the left side of the doorway.
The installation of the *kūrca* for the initiation of the *samayin* and *putraka* begins with the name of Skanda;
[one performs] three separate libations (*tarpaṇa*) each for Skanda, the Sādhaka, the Ācārya, Mṛtāyīśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta.
The offering of multiple funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the deceased, ritual bathing, libations (*tarpaṇa*) according to the prescribed number,

and the festive meal (*vṛddhibhojana*) must be performed. On the second day and subsequent days as well, one should perform the libations with an increase of one each time (*ekottaravṛddhi*), as well as the offering of rice-balls.
The number of libations (tarpaṇa) and the meals for the increase [of the ancestors] (vṛddhibhojana) should be performed.
On the fourth, fifth, and ninth days, there is one *navaśrāddha* at the conclusion of the *vṛddhibhojana*; on the eleventh day, there is another *navaśrāddha*.

On any one of the first, third, fifth, seventh, or ninth days, the collection of bones (*asthisañcayana*) should be performed; on the final day of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), the placement of stones and the removal from the cremation ground (*vīrādvāsana*) must be carried out. On the day immediately following the period of impurity, the great *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is to be performed.

The fifteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites must be performed. On the day following the *ekoddiṣṭas*, for those who have died as *samayins* or *putrakas*, the rite consisting of the union with Skanda, Caṇḍa, and Gaṇeśa is performed; for *sādhakas* and *ācāryas*, the rite consisting of the union with Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta is performed.

The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite must be performed. By means of this *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, once the connection with the state of being a deceased ancestor (*adhas-sambandha*) has been removed, for the duration of one year, the *udakumbha-śrāddha*, the fifteen monthly rites, the annual rites, the *aṣṭaka* rites, and the *śiva-śrāddha*s [are to be observed].
All these [rites] must be performed.
This entire [procedure] is explained in detail in the *Kāmika* [Tantra] regarding the fourth, fifth, and ninth [days], as follows:
One should give the gift of clothing to cover the naked to a consecrated householder;
at the conclusion of the cremation, one should offer [the rite] dedicated to the deceased, consisting of cloth and rice.
According to the method described for the *pīṭha* and *piṭhaka*, the preceptor should perform the rite with three girdles;
he should then fashion a new pit in front, measuring one *tāla* in depth.
Having smeared [the site] with water from the *homa* vessel, one should place in the center of the pedestal either a *kūrca* grass-bundle measuring a span (*prādeśa*) or simply a hollow pit.
Having fashioned a brick, a stone, or a clay bowl, and having placed it there along with the bundle of grass (kūrca) previously described,
one should perform this rite therein.
One who desires [results] should offer libations (tarpaṇa) every day individually by the names of Īśa, Skanda, and the others.
On the first day, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed three times.
One should increase [the number] by one each day individually up to twelve; the libation (tarpaṇa) for every meal is stated to be seventy-five in number.
One should satisfy one hundred and five [ancestors]; for a Brāhmaṇa, there are ten piṇḍas, while for a Kṣatriya, twelve are prescribed.
Fifteen days are prescribed for a Vaiśya, and thirty are proclaimed for a Śūdra; as long as their period of impurity lasts, so long must the rites of offering rice-balls and water be performed.
And all of this, accompanied by the word "svadhā" and [recited] with his name, one should offer on the fourth or fifth day, or on the ninth,
eleventh, or twelfth day.
That which is given with reference to one who has died is known as the *tadvaśrāddha* (the śrāddha for that person); the *navaśrāddha* (the first-anniversary śrāddha),
however, is devoid of both mantras, rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and water-libations.
Devoid of water, honey, and flowers, and abandoned by perfumes and garlands, [the offering] should be placed in nine earthen vessels for one, three, five, seven, or nine days.
The collection of bones for the Brahmins and others may be performed either sequentially or on the third day; thereafter, one should perform the *sañcayana* (the piling up of the bones).
Having removed the deceased from that place, one should take the funeral cake (piṇḍa) together with flowers, along with its grass-mat (kūrca),
a brick, a stone, or yellow pigment.

O twice-born ones, one should place the musical instrument together with the [other items] in the middle of the sacred water; then, when the desire has been expressed, the ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed.
On the eleventh day, or after three fortnights, or likewise every month; at the end of the year, or after six months, it is joined with the annual [śrāddha].
It is said that there are sixteen śrāddhas; whatever gift is offered among these, on the second day, one should perform the ekoddiṣṭa and the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
For one whose sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite occurs before the completion of a year from the date of death,
one should continue to offer food along with a water-pot for the duration of that year.
Furthermore, regarding the completion of the *piṇḍa* offerings over three days starting from the cremation and so forth: on the first day, one *piṇḍa* is offered;
on the second, four; and on the third, five should be given. As stated in the *Kāmika*:
"On the first [day], however, there is one *piṇḍa*; likewise, on the second, four; and on the third, five."
One should give it for three days; this is the procedure for one who is not ill.
Thus, within the ten-day period, if either of two women in their courses drinks [the water],
for all *sapiṇḍas* other than the legitimate (*aurasa*) son, it is in that very same manner.
The completion of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) offering must be performed. Thus says the Smṛti:

"If an equinox (saṃkrānti) or a new moon (darśa) should occur within the ten-day period, the water and the rice-ball offering should be completed on that day; however, for others, it should be done on the following day."
In this regard, the offering of water with sesame seeds (tilodaka) must be performed daily by members of all four castes for as long as the period of impurity lasts;
it may be done once, three times, or by increasing the number of handfuls (añjali) each day. Furthermore, in the *Kālottara*, the offering of water is described as follows:

Having cast the funeral ball (piṇḍa) into water or into fire according to one's inclination, and having offered sesame seeds and water upon the ground with the heart-mantra, the name [of the deceased], and the words "svadhā astu," [one should perform the rite].
The meaning is that for those whose names have been uttered, one should offer with the *hṛdaya* mantra, saying "svadhā.
And in the *Suprabheda*:
"Having gone to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) and performed the ritual bath according to the rule together with the *sapiṇḍas*..."
Water with sesame seeds should be offered, preceded by his name.
In the *Kāmika*, however, it is stated in a certain place regarding the libation (*tarpaṇa*):

"Then, having gone to a body of water and bathed, having spread out a seat with excellent *kuśa* grass, thereafter, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), [one recites] first the *praṇava*, the *hṛdaya*, and then the *śuddhāti-veśā*."

Having uttered the name ending with *dīśāntaparyanta*, then the name ending with *gaṇeśa* preceded by *skanda*, and then the word *vāk* followed by *bhava* for the west; then the practitioner, having said *atha aham*, should again perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) ending three times with *svadhā*.

In some places, the offering of sesame and water (*tilodaka*) is said to increase by one each day; that has already been demonstrated previously. Regarding the determination of the duration [of impurity], three positions have been presented:
that it lasts for one [offering] per day, another that it lasts for three [offerings] per day, and others [that it lasts for] a handful (*añjali*) per day.

"Others say [it is] for the sake of prosperity. All these funeral rites (*pretakarma*) must not be performed by a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) on behalf of his ancestors during his period of studentship. If he performs them, there occurs a re-initiation (*punarupanayana*) and so forth.
As the *Smṛti* states:

If a religious student (*brahmacārin*) performs the rites beginning with cremation and ending with the offering of the funeral rice-balls (*sapiṇḍana*), then— except in the case of his mother and father—

he must undergo re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*) before he may attain [the status of] a performer. However, in this [latter] case, the divine rites (*daiva-kriyā*) are primarily for the sons and others who have been initiated.

The performance [of the rite] should be carried out by the mantra-guru, or by the ancestors, or by the son, or even by the wife; it must not be performed by those who are undīkṣita (uninitiated). The status of the agent is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The śrāddha for the deceased must indeed be offered by the sons who are dīkṣita; by a kinsman..."
[The inheritance goes] to kinsmen, friends, disciples, servants, and initiated teachers.
In the absence of a son, however, the wife shall [inherit]; in the absence of a wife, however, the uterine brother.
Also in the *Kālottara*:

Indeed, the entire rite of consecration (saṃskāra), when performed by one who has not received initiation, must be carried out by a Guru, or else by a father, a son, or a wife; it should never be done by those who are uninitiated.
Through initiation, one becomes fit for hearing [the scriptures] and capable of performing worship; through initiation, one enters the stage of spiritual life.
But he obtains the dharmas according to his worthiness.

Through initiation (dīkṣā) knowledge is attained; through initiation one becomes a possessor of perfection (siddhi). One whose self is purified by the initiation of Śiva possesses the authority for that very [attainment] therein.
This too:
this Śrāddha consisting of mantra, endowed with knowledge and meditation.
The ritual for the accomplishment of the mantra of the gurus must be performed by those who know the samaya and so forth.

The performance of the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi) belongs to the preceptor (ācārya) and the others; it is stated in the Kālottara that in the absence of each preceding one, the next succeeding one performs it:
"By the preceptor for four, by the practitioner (sādhaka) for three, and by two..."
By the son himself, who knows the rules, for his own lineage.
Precisely because of the absence [of all else], the knower of the samaya should cause it to be performed by either the preceptor, the practitioner,
the spiritual son, or the initiate.
Alternatively, one may take the bones [of the deceased] and, having bathed the corpse, adorn it.
For those who have been initiated, the Śiva-śrāddha must be performed, as stated in the Jñānaratnāvalī:
This Śrāddha, as described, consists of initiation (dīkṣā) and bestows the [highest] state;
it must be performed by the son of Śaṅkara for those who have been initiated.

In this regard, for those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*), only the Śaiva *śrāddha* should be performed, and not the Vedic one; for if the Vedic rite were performed, they would not go to the world of Śiva. Furthermore, in the *Vīrabhadrasaṃhitā* it is stated:
"Upon the death of those who have been initiated, one should perform only the Śaiva *śrāddha*, and not the Vedic."
And in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"For those Śaivas who have been initiated, the funeral rite (*śrāddha*) must indeed be Śaiva alone.
This is stated in the *Kāraṇa*.
For these men who have been initiated by the five initiations, their death should be treated as that of a Śaiva;
one should perform the Śrāddha rite in this very manner.
p.
395) Here, it is said that [the rite] is not Vedic. And in the *Mohaśūrottara*: "For initiated Śaivas, the *śrāddha* should indeed be Śaiva alone; it is not..."

If the Vedic rite has been performed, one does not go to the world of Śiva. Furthermore, in the *Vīrabhadra-saṃhitā*, it is stated that for those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*), when they die, one should perform only the Śaiva *śrāddha*,
provided there is the performer’s faith— that is, the desire to perform the Vedic *śrāddha*— Śiva...
Immediately after performing the *śrāddha*, the Vedic *śrāddha* must be performed. As it is stated in that very same source:
"If that [Śaiva rite] is to be performed, then the Śaiva [rite] comes first, and thereafter the Vedic; such is the rule."
But it is not so stated in the Nandīśvarakāmika:
"When those who have attained perfection through Śiva-initiation die, one should first perform the Śiva-śrāddha, and afterwards the Vedic [śrāddha]."
By performing the Śiva-śrāddha for those very ancestors, even the fault of performing the Vedic śrāddha for one's mother occurs.
Regarding that very point:
"He who performs the Vedic śrāddha without having performed the Śiva-śrāddha..."
Both the initiated and the dead—these two go to hell.

Now, is the one who performs the consecration (*saṃskartā*) a follower of the Śiva-dharma (*śivadharmī*), a follower of the worldly dharma (*lokadharmī*), a spiritual son (*putraka*), or a initiate (*samayī*)? It cannot be the first, because since he is free from impurity (*aśauca*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of him having to offer funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and water libations (*udakadāna*); yet this is not accepted as the case. This is for the sake of conforming to worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*).

Because of the rule for offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). It cannot be the second [alternative], because that too would entail the consequence that the impurity lasts for three days and the rice-balls are obtained after exactly three days; and this is not an acceptable conclusion.

Because it contradicts established practice (*ācāra*). It is not the third [alternative], because even in the absence of a contradiction with practice, it is logically impossible for that very [entity] to be the agent by way of being a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Nor is this a desirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), since other [entities] are also seen to be agents. It is not the fourth [alternative], because among the various sub-sects of Śaivism...

For if there were impurity lasting more than twenty-five days, it would result in a contradiction with the established practice of completing the *piṇḍa* offerings [within that period]. Nor should it be argued that even if the performer of the rites (*saṃskartṛ*) is subject to impurity according to the *Śivadharma*, the offering of *piṇḍas* would still not take place due to the impurity caused by cremation— just as in the case of one observing celibacy (*brahmacarya*) upon the death of a father.

Because immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) results from a single bath, it is logically untenable for that bath to necessitate the offering of funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*) immediately thereafter. Nor is it the case that, even in the absence of impurity (*āśauca*) due to a female slave, the one who performs the cremation of a deceased student (*brahmacārin*) would be subject to the impurity prescribed for the specific caste of the deceased.
It should be stated that for one following the Śiva-dharma, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) must take place even during the period of impurity prescribed by birth-status;

for among the intermediate Śaivas, there arises a systematic arrangement wherein even the impurity prescribed by birth-status takes the form of thirty, twenty-five, five, three, or two days. Moreover, in the event of the death of a *putraka*...

Whether one follows the Śiva-dharma or the worldly dharma, it should be stated that [the impurity] resulting from cremation constitutes the full extent of the impurity; for among the intermediate Śaivas, the *putrakas* and *samayins* are those to be cremated.

Even though the performer’s additional period of impurity is rendered [neutralized] by the impurity of the cremation when serving as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāraka*), the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*) [is still required].

And for her [the widow], the completion of the three-day funeral rite (*piṇḍa*) occurs here as well; because those who follow the Śiva-dharma are not subject to impurity (*āśauca*), while those who follow the triple-worldly (*tri-loka*) dharma are subject to a three-day impurity. Nor does the impurity of one who has offered water (*sodaka*)—even if it be restricted—persist through the impurity of cremation (*dāha*).
It should not be said that the detailed period of impurity (*aśauca-vistara*) is [replaced] by the impurity of the *putraka* due to cremation;
for,
among the various types of cremations, when a *putraka* dies, there is an additional period of impurity for the *samayin* who performs the rite.

If it is argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of restricting [the period of impurity] due to the impurity caused by cremation (*dāha-āśauca*), we reply: It is established in all the scriptures that the impurity resulting from cremation is the motivator for the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa-dāna*), whereas the impurity resulting from death is the motivator for the mere offering of water (*udaka-dāna*).
Likewise, because there is an absence of *piṇḍas* for the *sapiṇḍas* other than the primary performer,

the mere offering of water (*udakadāna*) serves only to necessitate the suspension of ritual acts (*karmaparyudāsa*) due to the impurity (*āśauca*) occasioned by that [death], and this [offering of water]...

The number of days for impurity due to cremation determines the duration of impurity for death; it does not determine the duration of impurity for the death of one who is junior to the cremator. When a student (*brahmacārī*) dies, the three-day impurity of the *sodaka* (sapinda) is set aside for the cremator.
During the ten-day period of impurity for a father, although the periods of purification— namely the cremation, the end of the rites, three days, a pakṣiṇī, a day, and a night— are possible,
the impurity prescribed by birth is sometimes the determining factor, as it is for a householder regarding his slave.

In the event of the death of a father, for a son who is a *brahmacārī* and the performer of the cremation, regarding the impurity (*āśauca*) caused by the cremation, there is no scriptural injunction for the impurity pertaining to the father to apply to the cremator by taking into account a lower caste of the same genus; therefore, in reality, there is an absence of caste-based impurity (*jātyāśauca*).

[This refers to] the impurity (āśauca) caused by birth for one who follows worldly custom and is free from [Vedic] initiation, which arises simultaneously with the cooking [of the funeral cakes]; and that [impurity] is of one form among the three castes, yet it is of four kinds due to specific scriptural statements regarding the mother— consisting of thirty, twenty-five, and fifteen days— and likewise other forms of impurity.

It should not be said that there is no distinction, because for one who follows worldly custom, the rule of purification lasting three days is prescribed without reference to [specific] caste (*jāti*). (p. 398)

Because there is an absence of impurity based on birth (*jātyāśaucatva*); for one who is in reality a follower of worldly custom (*lokadharmin*) and free from *sūtaka*, since there is no existence of impurity caused by cooking together (*sahapāka-nimitta-āśauca*) that is prescribed by taking birth as the basis, there is an absence of impurity based on birth for one who is in reality a follower of worldly custom and free from *sūtaka*.

Because impurity resulting from eating together (*sahapāka*) is equal to impurity resulting from contact (*saṃparka*), there is this distinction: in the case of impurity due to contact, the impurity lasts for the number of days of the contact; however, in the case of impurity due to eating together, it lasts for the number of days of the person who cooked, as stated in that very [text]. Furthermore, upon the death of one who follows the Śiva-dharma, [the same applies] for one who follows the Śiva-dharma...

Since the burner possesses the nature of being burned, let there be no offering of rice-balls (*apiṇḍadāna*) due to the impurity arising from birth within the same lineage (*sajātīyaniṣṭhājāti*). Thus, how could there be a contradiction with established practice?
Furthermore, even though there is no contradiction between the Ādiśaivas and the Mahāśaivas or Anuśaivas, [this applies] regarding the intermediate Śaivas (*avāntaraśaiva*).
It should not be said that there is an infinite regress regarding caste; for even in that case, among those of the same class who possess the nature of Śiva—

namely, the *samayins* and *putrakas*— there is proximity through their connection to the Śiva-āśrama, and even when two *samayins* and *putrakas* have been accepted, there is [proximity] through their connection to the worship of Śiva.

In the case of impurity (*āśauca*) arising from the birth of a relative of the *saṃbandhayitṛ* (the one who effects the connection), the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*) is certainly not established;

for between the near and the distant [relatives], the near is to be taken, since it is established in both worldly custom and the Vedas that between the internal (*antaraṅga*) and the external (*bahiraṅga*), the internal is to be accepted. Thus...

In the event of the death of a *putraka*, even when he acts as the officiant (*saṃskartṛ*), there is no fault for those belonging to the intermediate Śaiva schools. Nor should it be argued that the impurity of the cremator’s *samaya* would be restricted by the impurity of the *putraka*; for such a restriction is accepted. This is because [the impurity] is removed by the consecration of the *putraka*, who is the foremost bearer of the worship of Śiva.

Because the contraction of impurity (*aśauca-saṃkoca*) is an ornament for the initiate (*samayin*), [it follows that] if there were no scriptural statement [to that effect], such a contraction of impurity would not be appropriate for him; or rather, let the Veda [be the authority]. (p. 399)

Likewise, what loss is there for us? Nor should it be argued that when there is an extensive period of impurity, the initiate (*samayin*) would be unable to perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite at the end of fifteen days upon the death of a "son" (*putraka*).
For even though impurity exists for the initiate at that time, the performer [of the rite] possesses temporary [purity].

Since the performance of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is established by the authority of the *smṛti* texts stating, "Purity, purity, and again he [is pure]," it follows that this is appropriate. If it is argued that, in that case, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* would not take place on the day immediately following, the answer is:
true; for even though it is possible there, there is another time, such as after three fortnights (*tripakṣa*), and so forth.
Because the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is established as being applicable there;

for all authorities accept that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* may be performed on the day immediately following the period of impurity (*āśauca*), or at another time if one travels after the period of impurity has ended. Therefore, by the impurity prescribed for the specific caste of the deceased...

In the determination of the period of impurity for one who has cremated [the corpse], there is never any doubt; thus, among the various types of impurity caused by such signs as mentioned, the ritual duties ending with the funeral rites—
including the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*— are governed by the impurity occasioned by the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite itself.
Upon completion, there is the purification of all sins for the primary performer;
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, he goes to the world of Śiva. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Those who do not perform these nine and sixteen *śrāddha* rites..."
Even by hundreds of śrāddha offerings performed for him, his state as a piśāca will endure for a long time.
At the gate, on a heap of ashes, and in the sky— in this sequence— he remains as a preta and plays for three days, three days, and one day respectively.
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, one goes to the world of Śiva. Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*.
Thus has been declared this secret, known as the supreme, which bestows the fruit of liberation and constitutes the purification for the devotees of Śiva, exactly as described.
He who was renowned as Vedajñāna Munīndra, himself Śiva, the propagator of the tradition of the secrets of the Śaiva Āgamas—
by his ascetic disciple, who bore that same name, for the sake of the Śaivas...
The Āśaucadīpikā has been composed for the purpose of [clarifying] its application.
Thus ends the *Āśaucadīpikā*, composed by Vedajñānadeva, a resident of Śrīmad-Vyāghrapurī.
